catalogTitle: ב - מוצאי ט' באב - מעשה רבי ר' אלימלך

oneLiner.en: Through the story of a disciple of Rebbe Reb Elimelech stranded on an island, the Rav teaches that wherever a Jew finds himself is a mission from Heaven.

abstract.en: The Rav tells a story, related by the Alexander Rebbe, about one of the yoshvim who sat and learned in Rebbe Reb Elimelech's beis medrash and received a weekly stipend. When his envelope began to shrink and then came empty, he understood it as a sign that he was no longer worthy, and after teshuvah and fasts did not help, his friends collected money and sent him overseas to trade. On the way home the ship left him behind on an island. Near death from thirst he found a little water, yet remembered he was a talmid of Rebbe Reb Elimelech and made a shehakol and a borei nefashos with great kavanah. Back in Lizhensk, the Rebbe told him two souls had waited on that island for hundreds of years for exactly those brachos. The Rav concludes that every place a person reaches is a shlichus, adds a second short story about a bracha on a drink, and says a Jew must never despair but use every moment there.

en: The disciple took his shrinking stipend as a sign from Rebbe Reb Elimelech that he was no longer worthy, and tried to correct himself with teshuvah and fasting.
Even near death from thirst, he held back and made a bracha with great kavanah before drinking, because he was a talmid of Rebbe Reb Elimelech.
Rebbe Reb Elimelech revealed that two souls had waited on that island for hundreds of years and were brought to their tikkun through his brachos.
The Rav teaches that everything a person does in a given place, which tree he learns under and which water he drinks, is a mission sent from Heaven.
A Jew must never despair; wherever he arrives he should use every moment for Torah, tefillah and chessed, knowing he is Hashem's messenger.

title.en: The disciple whose stipend shrank

summary.en: The Rav begins a story told by the Alexander Rebbe about the yoshvim in Rebbe Reb Elimelech's beis medrash, who got weekly money from the gabbai. One of them found less and less in his envelope and finally nothing; taking it as a sign that he was no longer worthy, he did teshuvah and fasted.

title.en: Sent overseas and left on an island

summary.en: He asks his friends for advice, and they collect money and send him overseas to trade. On the way back the ship stops at an island; absorbed in Tehillim under a tree he misses the ship's whistle and is left behind alone.

title.en: Thirst, and a brachah with kavanah

summary.en: Near death from thirst, he finds a little water; though a man in such a state becomes like an animal, he remembers he is a talmid of Rebbe Reb Elimelech and makes a shehakol and borei nefashos with great kavanah. When the ship returns he goes home to Lizhensk, and the Rebbe begins to tell him about two souls on the island.

title.en: The souls' tikkun; every place is a mission

summary.en: Rebbe Reb Elimelech explains that his brachos brought the souls to their tikkun and that he arranged the causes to send him there. The Rav draws from the passuk of a man's steps being set by Hashem that everything a person does is a shlichus, adds a short story about brandy drunk without a bracha, and concludes that a Jew must never despair but use every moment wherever he is sent.

catalogTitle: בענין התהפכות ירמיהו הנביא לשלמה המלך וט' באב לשמיני עצרת

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Yirmiyahu, the prophet of the churban, is a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, and that Tisha B'Av, the day of Yirmiyahu, will one day turn into Shemini Atzeres, the day of Shlomo.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Shemini Atzeres, the center of all the yomim tovim, and its haftorah, which says Shlomo HaMelech completed all he desired. No person achieves that, he says, but Shlomo, who ruled the world through wisdom and peace, brought down a model of the days of Moshiach. His era was the complete union of Hashem and Klal Yisroel, and Shemini Atzeres is his day. Tisha B'Av is its opposite, the day of the 'divorce', and Yirmiyahu is its soul. Citing the Chasam Sofer and the mekubalim, he explains that Yirmiyahu is a gilgul of Shlomo, sent back to see the destruction of the Temple he built. Therefore Tisha B'Av will become Shemini Atzeres. He shows this in the seudah hamafsekes on a Shabbos erev Tisha B'Av, the Pinchas maftir, the end of Masechta Taanis and the word 'moed' in Eicha, and calls on everyone, especially broken bochurim, to feel what is missing and bring Moshiach.

en: Shemini Atzeres is the center around which all the yomim tovim revolve, and it is the day of Shlomo HaMelech.
Shlomo ruled the whole world through wisdom and peace, without war, and his era was a model of the days of Moshiach.
Shlomo's time was the complete union of Hashem and Klal Yisroel, while Tisha B'Av is the day of separation, with Yirmiyahu as its soul.
Yirmiyahu is a gilgul of Shlomo, sent back to see the destruction of the Beis Hamikdash he himself built.
Since time and soul correspond, Tisha B'Av is a gilgul of Shemini Atzeres and will become the greatest yom tov.
On a Shabbos erev Tisha B'Av the seudah hamafsekes is eaten like the feast of Shlomo in his time, and Shlomo rather than Yirmiyahu is the guest.
The Rav says the small, lowly last generations will bring Moshiach, when they feel what is missing and add Torah, tefillah and guarding themselves.

candidateTopics: Tisha B'Av turning into a yom tov

title.en: Shemini Atzeres and Shlomo's completed desire

summary.en: After thanking Rav Twersky, the Rav describes Shemini Atzeres as the center of all the yomim tovim and the day of Shlomo HaMelech, and brings its haftorah that Shlomo completed all he desired. He asks how that can be, when no person achieves everything and the Midrash says Hashem Himself has not yet rejoiced in His works.

title.en: Shlomo's kingdom as a model of Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav answers that Shlomo became king of the world without war, through wisdom alone, as in the judgment of the two women, and his reign brought peace and abundance. Comparing it to the Rambam's description of the days of Moshiach, he concludes that Shlomo lifted his generation above the limits of time into a taste of Moshiach's days, when every desire can be fulfilled.

title.en: The full moon and Shlomo as soul of the union

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shlomo's era was the complete union of Hashem and Klal Yisroel, and that Tisha B'Av is its opposite, a 'divorce'. He brings the Midrash that the fifteen generations from Avraham to Shlomo parallel the waxing moon, which waned until Tzidkiyahu, and, using Sefer Yetzirah's parallel of time and soul, calls Shlomo, the author of Shir Hashirim, the soul of the union.

title.en: Yirmiyahu, the soul of Tisha B'Av

summary.en: The Rav calls Yirmiyahu the soul of Tisha B'Av: he cursed his birth and told Hashem He had persuaded him to become a prophet, yet he became the prophet of the churban. He brings the Midrash of the kohen who had to deal with a sotah who was his own mother, and applies it to Tziyon, the mother of Klal Yisroel, concluding that Shlomo and Yirmiyahu stand at opposite ends.

title.en: Yirmiyahu as a gilgul of Shlomo

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer, citing the mekubalim, that Yirmiyahu is a gilgul of Shlomo. Through the Gemara that Rome began to rise on the day Shlomo married Pharaoh's daughter, and Rashi's rule that Yerushalayim and Rome rise at each other's expense, he explains that the churban was decreed then, together with Shlomo's return as Yirmiyahu to witness it.

title.en: Tisha B'Av will become Shemini Atzeres

summary.en: Since Yirmiyahu is a gilgul of Shlomo, the Rav says, Tisha B'Av is a gilgul of Shemini Atzeres and will become the greatest yom tov; its mourning clothes will be exchanged for Shlomo's royal garments, Eicha will turn back into Shir Hashirim, and the fasts will become days of joy. He brings the Rebbe of Lublin's word, and the story of a tzaddik who on Tisha B'Av showed with tears how kiddush will be made on that day.

title.en: The special food of each yom tov

summary.en: The Rav explains that every major yom tov has its own food, like matzah on Pesach, so that the yom tov becomes part of a Jew's body and stays with him afterwards. Tisha B'Av also must be taken in, and for this Chazal instituted the seudah hamafsekes, which is itself part of Tisha B'Av.

title.en: This year's seudah: Shlomo as the guest

summary.en: At the seudah hamafsekes, the Rav says, Yirmiyahu comes as a guest with his Eicha. This year, when Tisha B'Av falls after Shabbos, a rare order of readings and haftoros, the Rav says, makes it a year of consolation, and Shlomo himself will sit at the table singing zemiros, as the Shulchan Aruch says one eats on such a Shabbos like the feast of Shlomo in his time.

title.en: Feeling the loss and adding one's share

summary.en: The Rav calls this a great kindness and a call to arousal, bringing the Rebbe of Lublin that the three Shabbosos of the three weeks parallel the three regalim, with Shemini Atzeres as the fourth. With a story of a 'hole in the pocket' he urges that the days before Shabbos be used to feel the loss of the Beis Hamikdash, add Torah, tzedakah and tefillah, and ask for malchus shamayim, malchus beis Dovid and the Beis Hamikdash.

title.en: Pinchas, the end of Taanis, and Shlomo's crown

summary.en: The Rav shows that in an ordinary year the maftir of Pinchas, about Shemini Atzeres, is followed at once by Divrei Yirmiyahu, joining the two. He then brings the end of Masechta Taanis, which closes on the day of Shlomo's wedding, and explains that Tisha B'Av only looks like a bill of divorce; Hashem tells the daughters of Tziyon to look at King Shlomo with the crown that will be placed on Moshiach.

title.en: The laughter of Moshiach and the small generations

summary.en: The Rav explains the laughter of 'then our mouths will be filled with laughter': the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Maggid, Rebbe Reb Elimelech and the Chozeh of Lublin tried to bring Moshiach and could not, and the lowly last generations will bring him. He calls on the yeshiva bochurim to feel that something is missing, not to say nothing is lacking, and stresses the worth of a young man today who learns, davens and guards himself amid all the tests.

title.en: Tisha B'Av, the hidden moed, and fallen bochurim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Maggid of Mezritch on souls that are like Shabbos, and the Rokeach's finding of all the yomim tovim in the parshiyos. One yom tov is not written there: Tisha B'Av, which is called a moed and has no tachanun. He compares it to a bochur with talents who fell through bad friends; he is a moed that fell, and he can catch himself and return.

title.en: Eicha turned to joy, and the closing blessing

summary.en: The Rav says this Shabbos leading into Tisha B'Av is a special time for broken bochurim, as Yirmiyahu becomes Shlomo and Tisha B'Av becomes Shemini Atzeres. He brings remazim on Eicha and on the 'bill of divorce', mentions that the Berditchever saw the third Beis Hamikdash every Shabbos Chazon, and closes with the blessing that through Torah, tefillah and good middos the fasts will become days of joy, as Zechariah promised.

catalogTitle: The Rejuvenation of the World and of Mankind

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Rosh Chodesh Nissan, when man was created, is the time each year when the world is renewed, and that a Jew must renew himself with it, become a true Adam, and bind himself to Hashem through the emunah of Pesach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the opinion that the world and man were created in Nissan, and describes Hashem's original plan for a perfect world without toil, illness or death. Adam HaRishon spoiled it with the sin of the Tree of Knowledge; Hashem began again with the Exodus and chose Klal Yisroel, who spoiled it with the Golden Calf; then He confined His holiness to the Mishkan, set up on Rosh Chodesh Nissan, which ended with the destruction of the Batei Mikdash. A fourth Rosh Chodesh Nissan is promised. Hashem allowed these failures to teach a Jew to start over after every failure. The Rav then describes how the world comes back to life each Nissan and calls on each person to renew himself, to master the animal traits of his mazal, and to become an Adam. Pesach, the festival of Avraham Avinu, is the time of emunah: the bond of chasan and kallah with Hashem, eaten in the matzah and transmitted to children.

en: Hashem's original plan in creating the world in Nissan was a perfect world where man would live forever, without toil, worry or illness.
The plan was disappointed three times: Adam's sin, the Golden Calf after Klal Yisroel was chosen, and the destruction of the Mishkan and the Batei Mikdash; a fourth Rosh Chodesh Nissan is promised.
Hashem allowed these failures as a lesson: a Jew who fails must not tire but do teshuvah and start over again, every time.
In Nissan the whole creation is reborn and sings a new song, and a person who stays the same old self is left out of it.
Each person is born with a mazal resembling an animal, and he must master that trait and raise it for avodas Hashem.
Pesach, the festival of Avraham Avinu, is the time of emunah, when Klal Yisroel became Hashem's kallah; matzah is the food of emunah.
Eating chametz on Pesach cuts a person off, like eating from the Tree of Knowledge, while keeping Pesach binds him to Hashem like eating from the Tree of Life.

title.en: Creation in Nissan and Hashem's original plan

summary.en: The Rav opens with Na'aseh adam said on Rosh Chodesh Nissan, following Rabbi Yehoshua that the world was created in Nissan, and mentions Birkas HaChamah every 28 years. He then describes Hashem's intention: a perfect world without worry, illness or toil, where man lives forever and learns Torah.

title.en: Three disappointments and a fourth Nissan

summary.en: The Rav explains that Adam's sin spoiled the plan, stressing that Hashem's 'disappointment' and 'regret' are said in human terms. Hashem began anew at the Exodus with Klal Yisroel, which the Golden Calf spoiled, and then confined His holiness to the Mishkan set up on Rosh Chodesh Nissan, which ended in destruction; a fourth Rosh Chodesh Nissan with the third Beis HaMikdash is promised.

title.en: The lesson: start over again

summary.en: The Rav asks why Hashem allowed three disappointments if He knew what would happen, and compares it to the Rosh Chodesh offering brought as an atonement for Hashem for diminishing the moon. He answers that it is a lesson: a Jew who fails in his avodah must not tire but do teshuvah and start over, again and again.

title.en: The world is reborn each Nissan

summary.en: The Rav explains that the newness of creation descends every Nissan, and paints the spring with the words of Shir HaShirim: the white shrouds of winter melt into green fields, flowers, birds and butterflies, and all of creation sings a new song to Hashem. He asks why man should stay the same old self while everything renews itself, and calls on each person to wake up and decide to be an Adam, not a beast.

title.en: Mastering the animal in man; renewal for Pesach

summary.en: The Rav explains that each person is born under a mazal like the animals of the shevatim's brachos, and must be master over that trait and raise it for avodas Hashem. He adds that Nissan is a time of techiyas hameisim, and that everything on Pesach is new, from clothing to dishes, so a person should want to be new as well.

title.en: Avraham Avinu, emunah and matzah

summary.en: The Rav brings that Pesach corresponds to Avraham Avinu, who baked matzos on Pesach, and that emunah is his inheritance to every Jew, hidden or revealed. Emunah is tied to Yetzias Mitzrayim, when Klal Yisroel became Hashem's kallah, with seven brachos at the Seder like sheva brachos; matzah is the food of emunah.

title.en: The bond of Pesach and the sin of chametz

summary.en: The Rav explains that emunah is transmitted to children through the Haggadah, and asks why only chametz on Pesach carries kares while transgressions on Shavuos and Sukkos do not. He answers that Pesach is the bond of chasan and kallah with Hashem, so chametz cuts one off, and brings from the sefarim that chametz and se'or equal the gematria of the Tree of Knowledge, while matzah is like eating from the Tree of Life.

title.en: Making a memorable Pesach

summary.en: The Rav urges using the Yom Tov with yiras Shamayim and simchah: being scrupulous about Pesach food, saying the Haggadah and Hallel and eating matzah with joy, which gives emunah that lasts a lifetime. He mentions that the heavenly family comes to the Seder, brings Reb Chaim Meir of Vizhnitz on making a Pesach to remember, and thanks the yeshivah for the chance to speak.

catalogTitle: צריכים להרגיש יותר הצער של שריפת בית אלוקינו; ולהיות מובדל מפגמים דקים

oneLiner.en: Taking the fire that broke out the day before as a message from Hashem, the Rav calls for feeling the burning of the Beis HaMikdash more deeply and for 'making havdalah' again and again, separating oneself even from fine flaws.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Rambam that crying out to Hashem in every trouble is a path of teshuvah, and that calling a trouble chance is cruelty. Every passuk speaks to every generation, and this week's 'a people heard the voice of G-d speaking from the fire' speaks to the fire that broke out in the camp the day before. He tells how the kabbalists of Jerusalem brought about the takanah against music at Jerusalem weddings, because the churban is felt more there; the Nine Days are such a time, and one must feel the burning of the Beis HaMikdash. A mashal of the king's violinist shows why Torah study is so precious, and the fire disrupted learning. He then explains the segulah of relighting the havdalah candle: fire does not distinguish, so one who keeps distinguishing more finely is saved from fire. He applies this to refinement in Shabbos, tefillah and going beyond the letter of the law, and closes with gratitude for the miracles and the promise of consolation.

en: Following the Rambam, the Rav teaches that troubles are signals from Heaven; calling them chance is cruelty that brings more troubles.
The fire in the camp is Hashem speaking 'from within the fire', and a person with sense must understand one thing from another.
There are places and times, Jerusalem and the Nine Days, where the churban must be felt more, and the Rav says each person according to his level should feel the burning of the Beis HaMikdash more.
Fire does not distinguish, so the remedy for fire is havdalah: making ever finer distinctions, as with a torch rather than a small candle.
A refined Jew does not settle for fulfilling his obligation; he goes beyond the letter of the law and responds to Hashem's hints.
One should become 'rich' from the fire in Torah, yiras shamayim and fine observance, and thank Hashem for the miracles that came with it.

title.en: The Rambam: troubles are not chance

summary.en: The Rav reads the opening of the Rambam's Hilchos Taaniyos: crying out in trouble is a path of teshuvah, and calling it chance is cruelty. He applies this week's passuk 'speaking from within the fire' to the fire in the camp the day before, a signal not to be taken lightly.

title.en: No music at Jerusalem weddings

summary.en: The Rav tells how, during an epidemic in Jerusalem, Rabbi Meir Auerbach learned through a she'elas chalom that the Kosel is where mourning for Jerusalem must be greater, and how the rabbanim enacted that no instruments be played at weddings in Jerusalem. A wealthy man who defied the takanah suffered a frightening punishment.

title.en: Feeling the burning of the Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: Just as there is a place, there is a time when the churban is felt more: the Nine Days. The Rav rebukes himself and the camp for carrying on as usual, asks them to picture the fire on Har HaBayis, and reads the repeated small fires as a reminder from Heaven, calling for 'let us search our ways'.

title.en: The king's violinist and bitul Torah

summary.en: On 'for what was the land lost... because they forsook My Torah' the Rav brings a mashal of a king who ignored his violinist's crimes until he could no longer play. Torah study is what would bring the other sins to be repaired; since the fire disrupted the learning in the camp, it is a call to strengthen Torah.

title.en: Havdalah again: a segulah against fire

summary.en: The Rav explains the custom of relighting the havdalah candle as a segulah against fire. Havdalah requires da'as; a coarse person distinguishes only gross differences, as by a small candle, while a refined Jew uses a torch to see fine ones. Fire does not distinguish, so one who keeps making havdalah is saved from fire, measure for measure.

title.en: Refinement beyond the obligation

summary.en: The Rav asks each one to demand more of himself: even the weekday brachos of Shemoneh Esreh should feel different on Shabbos, as shown by the ger tzedek who asked the Vilna Gaon how one could not recognize Shabbos in the desert. Citing the Mesillas Yesharim and the example of tevilah, he explains that serving from love means following hints, and that Jerusalem was destroyed because they kept to the letter of the law.

title.en: Each Jew is a Jerusalem

summary.en: Wherever there is yiras shamayim there is Jerusalem, so each Jew must rebuild the Mikdash in his heart and go beyond the letter of the law. A fire that does not distinguish came because they did not; the fire in the camp asks for more havdalah, with great da'as, again and again, and for seeing everything as hashgachah pratis.

title.en: Becoming rich after the fire; thanks and consolation

summary.en: The Rav asks that the fire make everyone richer in yiras shamayim and Torah. He contrasts the enemies who ran to defile the sifrei Torah with the bochurim who ran to save them, thanks Hashem for the miracles, and closes with Hashem's promise to rebuild Zion with fire and console doubly.

catalogTitle: דרוש נפלא בענין ט' באב שחל בשבת וטובת הגלות' והאיך הגלות מושרש בגאולה

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows that the exile of Av is rooted in the redemption of Nissan, that the hidden sparks and forgotten souls of the exile are the seeds of Moshiach, and that on Shabbos Nachamu one must accept the prophet's consolation with emunah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with 'Nachamu nachamu ami' after yet another Tisha B'Av and asks what 'ki mal'ah tzva'ah' means. He describes the yearly cycle of rising and falling, with Tammuz and Av given to Esav. From the rare trop 'yerach ben yomo', found only in Masei and serving the 'karnei parah' that is sung like a 'pazer', he builds his theme: following the Maharal, exile is rooted in redemption. Av, the month of Shimon and the lion, draws its blessing from Nissan, the month of Yehudah, whose every day is fresh like 'ben yomo'. The divided cow's horn of Av becomes the shofar of Moshiach. Yaakov's gift to Esav and the gid hanasheh stand for forgotten souls that will return; Dinah in Shechem held the spark of Moshiach ben Yosef. Exile is a mission to gather sparks. He ends with emunah in the redemption, the seven weeks of consolation, Tu B'Av, and receiving Yeshaya's good tidings.

en: Following the Maharal, every exile is rooted in redemption, and the purpose of exile is the geulah.
Av, the month of Shimon, receives its blessing from Nissan, the month of Yehudah, just as Shimon was blessed and given his inheritance within Yehudah's.
The 'karnei parah' of Av stands for division and exile, but joined with the 'yerach ben yomo' of Nissan it becomes the shofar of Moshiach.
Yaakov's gift to Esav and the gid hanasheh represent forgotten Jewish souls that fell under Esav, and they must all return.
The exile is not only a punishment but a mission from Hashem to gather the sparks scattered among the nations.
Although another Tisha B'Av has passed, one may not lose emunah; Moshiach will not delay once everything is complete.

title.en: Nachamu after another Tisha B'Av; the cycle of the year

summary.en: The Rav opens with Hashem's command to the prophet to comfort His people after yet another Tisha B'Av, and asks what 'ki mal'ah tzva'ah' means. He describes the yearly cycle of rising and falling, with Teves, Tammuz and Av given to Esav, down to Tisha B'Av and up again from the fifteenth of Av.

title.en: The rare trop 'yerach ben yomo' in Masei

summary.en: The Rav notes that the only 'yerach ben yomo' in the Torah appears in Masei, serving the 'karnei parah', which the Masorah says is sung like a 'pazer', and asks why it is needed and why it falls on the first Shabbos of Av. He brings the Midrash that the first day of Pesach and Tisha B'Av fall on the same day of the week.

title.en: Exile rooted in redemption: Av and Nissan

summary.en: The Rav brings the Maharal that exile is rooted in redemption, with Yocheved born as the Egyptian exile began and Moshiach born on Tisha B'Av. Through the Bnei Yissaschar he shows that Av, the month of Shimon, draws its blessing from Nissan, the month of Yehudah, and that the lion of Av hides chesed beneath gevurah.

title.en: The seven 'pazers' and the cow's horn

summary.en: The Rav explains that the descent begins in Sivan, when Behaaloscha with its seven 'pazers' is read, and that 'pazer', scattering, is exile whose inner side is redemption. From the Mishnah that a cow's horn is unfit for a shofar, since it is made of layers, he explains that the shofar means unity and the ingathering, while the 'karnei parah' means division, the cause of the exile.

title.en: Nissan: every day a new Rosh Chodesh

summary.en: The Rav brings the Shelah that every day of Nissan has the holiness of Rosh Chodesh, and explains it through the halachic idea of 'ben yomo', something still fresh from the same day. Nissan, the month of freshness, serves Av and gives it its blessing, as Yehudah gives to Shimon.

title.en: From cow's horn to the shofar of Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav explains that Av lacks the quality of Rosh Chodesh, and that in Matos-Masei the 'yerach ben yomo' of Nissan serves the 'karnei parah' of Av, turning it into the shofar of Moshiach. He adds that the 'migrash' around the Levite cities, from 'gerushin', alludes to exile, yet it remains joined to the city.

title.en: Hashem's ever-fresh love and the vessels of Midian

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem's love for Klal Yisroel never fades but is fresh every day like 'ben yomo'. He asks why the vessels of Midian needed kashering even when not 'ben yomo', and answers that Bilaam, Moav and Midian tried to spoil this love, so measure for measure their impurity is always fresh.

title.en: Yaakov's gift to Esav and the gid hanasheh

summary.en: The Rav explains that Tammuz and Av belong to Esav, and that the animals Yaakov sent Esav were Jewish souls, weak ones, that he was forced to place under Esav's rule. Yaakov's injured gid hanasheh, which sforim link to Tisha B'Av, stands for forgotten souls, yet like a mother who cannot forget her child, they must all return.

title.en: Dinah, Osnas and Moshiach ben Yosef

summary.en: The Rav tells the Midrash that from Dinah's captivity in Shechem was born Osnas, who was carried to Egypt, raised by Potiphar and became Yosef's wife and the mother of Moshiach ben Yosef. As a spark of Moshiach ben David lay in Moav, a great treasure lay in Shechem, and likewise in Tisha B'Av.

title.en: Exile to gather sparks

summary.en: The Rav sets the seven haftaros of consolation against the seven 'pazers', and brings the Ramchal that Hashem's plan is carried out even through sins, and the Gemara that Hashem scattered Israel among the nations to gain converts. The forgotten souls of the gid hanasheh fell among the nations, and in the days of Moshiach Esav will have to return the 'minchah'.

title.en: Why Dinah was taken: Hashem's plan

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ohr HaChaim that Hashem sometimes lets tzaddikim slip slightly so they will descend to raise holiness, and explains that Shechem ben Chamor held a holy spark of Moshiach ben Yosef. Through gematriaos and the Midrash that Dinah was first formed as Yosef, he shows Dinah was born to redeem that spark, and that she went out for the sake of Heaven.

title.en: Tisha B'Av on Shabbos heals the gid hanasheh

summary.en: The Rav explains that Tisha B'Av is the day of the gid hanasheh in time as Shechem is in place, and brings the Edom stanza of 'Baruch Hashem yom yom' ending 'ki lo yiznach l'olam Hashem'. This year, when Pesach and Tisha B'Av fell on Shabbos, Shabbos heals the gid hanasheh as Yaakov arrived 'shalem' on Shabbos, and the days of Av hold great hidden treasures.

title.en: Exile as a mission; the seven weeks of consolation

summary.en: The Rav describes Shabbos Nachamu as the visit of a great guest, Yeshaya the prophet, for whom one must prepare. He stresses that exile is not merely punishment but a mission to gather the sparks, which is what 'ki mal'ah tzva'ah' means, and counts fifty days from the eleventh of Av to Rosh Hashanah, seven weeks of consolation.

title.en: Waiting with emunah; the greatness of exile revealed

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban that since all the prophecies of exile came true, its promised end will surely come too; one may not lose emunah, as Hashem asks His people to wait and Moshiach will not delay. He cites the Shomer Emunim's practice of a daily immersion for the holiness of Moshiach, and describes how, when Moshiach comes, the greatness of Israel in exile will be revealed even to the nations.

title.en: Tu B'Av: rising from the grave, the full moon

summary.en: The Rav tells that in the desert people died every Tisha B'Av, and in the last year none died; on the fifteenth of Av, seeing the full moon, they knew the decree had ended and the day became a Yom Tov. Tisha B'Av is the diminished moon, and on the fifteenth of Av a Jew must rise from his 'grave' and serve Hashem.

title.en: Receiving the good tidings of Yeshaya

summary.en: The Rav closes that on Shabbos Nachamu Yeshaya comes with good tidings for Yerushalayim. He brings the Me'or Einayim that one who announces good news, and one who receives it, gains a spark of Eliyahu HaNavi, an auspicious time for teshuvah, so one should receive the prophet's consolation and become an ehrlicher Yid.

catalogTitle: "בחור שא נא עיניך" - להעלות הגשמיות (קליפות נוגה)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Three Weeks are a 'milah' that cuts away the three impure kelipos, while the week ending on the fifteenth of Av is the 'periah' that elevates kelipas nogah, the body, so that from then on a Jew must raise his eyes and serve Hashem even with his physical life.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Mishnah that the fifteenth of Av was a great Yom Tov, when the girls said 'bachur, sa na einecha', and the Gemara's reasons for it. He then brings the four kelipos of Yechezkel's vision and the Bnei Yissaschar's explanation of milah: three layers are cut off, like the three wholly impure kelipos, while the fourth, periah, is kelipas nogah, which can be turned to good, and the Tanya says a Jewish body comes from nogah. A goy can serve Hashem only by renouncing, like an olah; a Jew can elevate his eating, like a shelamim. The same pattern appears in orlah and neta revai. The Three Weeks are the milah of the season, and the week up to the fifteenth of Av is the periah, so it is a day of joy and the start of preparing for Rosh Hashanah. A ben Torah must refine his eating and conduct, make brachos with feeling, and love his friends, which repairs the sinas chinam behind the Churban.

en: Following the Bnei Yissaschar, milah cuts off three layers that correspond to the three wholly impure kelipos, while periah elevates the fourth layer, which corresponds to kelipas nogah.
A Jew's body is from kelipas nogah and can be turned to good, so a Jew can serve Hashem with his bodily powers, which a goy cannot do.
The Three Weeks are the milah of the season, cutting off through fasts and restrictions, and the week up to the fifteenth of Av is its periah; the fifteenth of Av is the joy of a completed bris.
'Bachur, sa na einecha' teaches that from the fifteenth of Av one must lift one's eyes: it is not enough to avoid the forbidden, a ben Torah must bring refinement into his eating and conduct.
The fifteenth of Av repairs the sinas chinam that caused the Churban; it is a time of love among friends, seeing only another's good.
When Jews say kedushah and daven together below, the angels can say kedushah above, so each person must come on time and start together with the minyan.

title.en: The Mishnah and the Gemara's reasons for the fifteenth of Av

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Mishnah that the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur were the greatest days of joy, and goes through the Gemara's reasons: the tribes were allowed to intermarry, the tribe of Binyamin was permitted again, and wood-cutting for the altar ended. He adds that from then the nights grow longer, so one must add learning at night.

title.en: Kelipas nogah and the layers of milah

summary.en: The Rav brings the four kelipos of Yechezkel's vision, the last being nogah, and the Bnei Yissaschar's teaching that milah cuts three layers while periah turns the fourth to good. With the Tanya, that a Jewish body is from nogah, he explains why the descendants of Keturah have milah but not periah.

title.en: Olah and shelamim, Noach's bris and Avraham's

summary.en: Through the Midrash on 'uri tzafon u'vo'i teiman' the Rav contrasts the olah, burnt entirely, with the shelamim, which is eaten: a goy can serve only by renouncing, a Jew can elevate his eating. He shows the same pattern in the four words of the brachah against the slanderers, in the bris with Noach versus the bris with Avraham, and in orlah and neta revai.

title.en: The Three Weeks as milah, the fourth week as periah

summary.en: The Rav explains that from Shiva Asar b'Tammuz there are really four weeks: the three until Tisha b'Av are the milah, cutting off with fasts and restrictions, and the week ending on the fifteenth of Av is the periah. Then, as at a bris, malchus shamayim is revealed, the preparation for Rosh Hashanah begins, and like metzitzah from the distant places, even the bodily powers are drawn close to Hashem.

title.en: From arur to baruch: the two halves of Av

summary.en: The Rav reads 'tze'enah ur'enah' as the revelation of the crown on the fifteenth of Av, and brings the Kedushas Levi that Av stands for arur and baruch, the first half belonging to Esav and the second to Yaakov. He reconciles this with the milah of Tisha b'Av as two steps, and contrasts the fasts and restrictions of the Three Weeks with the wine, meat and shidduchim of the fifteenth of Av.

title.en: 'Bachur, sa na einecha': lifting the eyes

summary.en: The Rav explains that a bachur who wants to learn normally guards his eyes, but on the fifteenth of Av he is told to lift them: even bodily matters must be done with elevation. Doing only what is permitted is not enough; a ben Torah must eat, dress and walk with refinement, as the Shulchan Aruch and the Rambam describe, until the body becomes like a window that lets the light through, which is what nogah means.

title.en: Neta revai: eating the Yerushalayim way

summary.en: The Rav explains that the fruit of the fourth year is not simply permitted; it must be brought to Yerushalayim and eaten there, which brings to yiras shamayim. Eating must be a 'Yerushalayim eating', with the refinement fitting a talmid chacham, and Torah and holy conduct each strengthen the other; the light of 'day' is the work of tzaddikim.

title.en: Brachos and eating as avodah

summary.en: The Rav says that from the fifteenth of Av one must bring kedushah into the night and the body as well. Brachos on food are learned from neta revai eaten in Yerushalayim; the Rambam says brachos are to remember Hashem, so a brachah must not be swallowed, and every bite can be a thanks. Chassidim eat dressed with a jacket and hat because eating is an avodah, and in this way malchus shamayim is revealed even in physical things.

title.en: Ahavas chaverim repairs the Churban

summary.en: The Rav explains that the fifteenth of Av, after the Three Weeks, repairs the sinas chinam that destroyed the Beis HaMikdash. He reads the permission for the tribes to intermarry and the return of Binyamin as ahavas chaverim, brings Rebbe Reb Elimelech's tefillah to see only a friend's good, and explains tov v'hameitiv as a brachah said only with another. Success in Torah and tefillah comes from being together, as in the letter about Rebbe Reb Elimelech's circle.

title.en: Kedushah above depends on kedushah below

summary.en: The Rav praises the yeshiva as a place of growth and urges going beyond the letter of the law. He brings the Nefesh HaChaim that everything above follows what Jews do below: the angels can say kedushah only when Jews say it together. So every bachur must come to davening on time and begin together with everyone, receiving from and giving to one another, as the angels do.

title.en: The taste of a refined body and Shabbos Nachamu

summary.en: The Rav says that one who refines his body and holds together with friends tastes Gemara, Shabbos and tefillah, and tells of a tzaddik who said that a poritz's lavish pleasure cannot compare to what he feels saying Nishmas. Such a person can feel the consolation of 'nachamu nachamu ami' on Shabbos Nachamu; the Rav closes with advice to learn before davening and a tefillah to pass, with the days of Av, from arur to baruch.

catalogTitle: מצה - A Food of אמונה and גאולה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that matzah is a food of emunah and of geulah, and that through the mitzvos of Pesach, from burning the chametz to eating the matzah and spilling the wine, the Jewish people wage their real war against their enemies.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying that this Pesach comes at a time of war against the Jewish people, and that Jews fight not with weapons but with Torah, tefillah, tzedakah and the mitzvos of Pesach. Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, whose trait is emunah, and the Zohar calls matzah the food of emunah. Bread contains all ten utterances of creation, while matzah, by gematria three times the filled-out Name of Hashem and three times geulah, holds the Names of the redemption itself. Our matzah is the same matzah the Jews ate in Mitzrayim, and on the Seder night the root of the soul is in Yerushalayim. The Rav then speaks of Pesach as the beginning, of Nissan as a month of healing, of matzah as the key that opens the treasuries of blessing, of the four cups and the plagues, and of searching and burning the chametz, which this year falls on Shabbos, as the battle against Amalek and Yishmael.

en: The Rav says the Jewish people wage war not with weapons but with Torah, tefillah, tzedakah and by keeping Pesach; the front is not far away but right here.
Pesach is the Yom Tov of Avraham Avinu, whose trait is emunah, and matzah is called the food of emunah.
Lechem equals three times the Name Havaya (78), while matzah equals three times the filled-out Name (45), which is also the value of geulah, so matzah carries the Names of the redemption.
The matzah eaten today is the same matzah the Jews ate in Mitzrayim, and on the Seder night the root of the soul goes to Yerushalayim and eats it there.
Matzah is the key that opens the treasuries of blessing on the Seder night.
Searching and burning the chametz is the inner war against the yetzer hara and against the klipah of Amalek, Esav and Yishmael, and this year it is strengthened by the power of Shabbos.

title.en: A Pesach of war

summary.en: The Rav says this Pesach comes while the Jews are in a state of war, and explains that Jews fight with Torah, tefillah, tzedakah, Hallel and the Haggadah, not with weapons. He brings the Targum on Eichah about the shouts of the nations on the Har HaBayis, which are countered with tefillah.

title.en: Pesach, Avraham Avinu and emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the three Yamim Tovim correspond to the Avos and that Pesach belongs to Avraham Avinu, in whose life many events took place on Pesach. Avraham's trait is emunah, Pesach is the time to implant emunah in one's children and oneself, and matzah is a food that contains emunah.

title.en: Bread, matzah and the Names of geulah

summary.en: Like a scientist who sees what is inside a food, the Rav explains that bread contains all ten utterances of creation and equals three times the Name Havaya. Matzah equals three times the filled-out Name, 45, which is also the value of geulah, so it holds the Names with which Hashem redeemed the Jews from Mitzrayim, and the Zohar calls it a food of emunah and of healing.

title.en: The same matzah as in Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Rav asks what a piece of the matzah baked in Mitzrayim would be worth if an archaeologist found it, and answers that our matzah is that very matzah, since its holy Names are the same. He brings the Targum Yonasan that the clouds of glory carried the Jews to Yerushalayim to eat the Korban Pesach, and says that on the Seder night the root of the soul goes to Yerushalayim.

title.en: Believing is greater than seeing

summary.en: The Rav tells of a Galician tzaddik who boasted to the Kotzker that he sees the Ushpizin, and the Kotzker's answer that he believes they come, and believing is greater than seeing. So too, with emunah a Jew is in Yerushalayim at the Seder; matzah belongs to Avraham Avinu, and emunah, as the Rambam and Ramban discuss, is the foundation of all the mitzvos.

title.en: Pesach as the beginning, and kareis

summary.en: The Rav explains that in the order of levels Pesach is the smallest Yom Tov, which is why only half Hallel is said, but it is the beginning, like Avraham Avinu. He shows from the punishment of kareis for chametz, which has no parallel on Shavuos and Sukkos, and from the kareis for Pesach and milah, that Pesach binds a Jew to Hashem with emunah.

title.en: Nissan, healing and Yitzchak's blessing

summary.en: After a break, the Rav brings the sefarim that Nissan is a month of healing between Adar and Iyar, whose initials spell the verse about Hashem as healer, and adds that matzah makes Nissan a month of emunah and healing in its own right. He brings the Targum Yonasan that Yitzchak blessed on the night of Pesach, when the treasuries of dew open, and Rashi that Yaakov's two kids were a Pesach and a Chagigah.

title.en: Matzah, the key to the treasuries

summary.en: The Rav explains that the treasuries of dew open on the Seder night, which is why Tal is said the next morning, and brings the Chasam Sofer's reading of grain, wine and oil as halachah, aggadah and the secrets of Torah. All these blessings open with the matzah, which the Targum calls by a word meaning opening, and this is why some have the custom of marking the challah with a key on the Shabbos after Pesach.

title.en: The four cups and the plagues

summary.en: The Rav brings two reasons for the four cups, the four mentions of a cup in the butler's dream and the four expressions of geulah, and explains that each plague was a blow to Mitzrayim and a healing for the Jews. Wine is spilled at the plagues because that is the bad part, and the Haggadah keeps multiplying the plagues because saying them activates them, which is the Seder's war against the klipah.

title.en: Searching and burning the chametz

summary.en: The Rav explains that the ten pieces of chametz in the search correspond to the ten utterances and the ten powers of the soul, and that the inner meaning of the search is to remove the yetzer hara from the heart. He tells of Rabbi Yisrael of Vizhnitz asking a chassid to search his heart for chametz, and says that burning the chametz is a call for Hashem to burn the chametz of the world, the ten nations and above all Amalek.

title.en: Biur chametz on Shabbos against Esav and Yishmael

summary.en: The Rav explains that this year the chametz is nullified on Shabbos, and the power of Shabbos is great against Amalek, who works today through Yishmael. He shows that tashbisu equals Shema Yisrael and that Vaizasa, the last son of Haman, equals Moshiach ben David, brings the Gemara and the Bnei Yissaschar on the zarzir and the orev, tells a story of a simple Jew's tefillah that annulled a decree, and ends with a blessing to eat the Pesach offerings in Yerushalayim.

catalogTitle: זמן של שישו אתה כל המתאבלים עליה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Tu b'Av is a festival of the future: Jews rejoice that they merited to mourn the Beis HaMikdash and never stopped hoping, and its full meaning will be revealed only when Moshiach comes.

abstract.en: The Rav notes that Pesach, head of the festivals, sets the weekday of each festival through the atbash sign, yet the seventh day of Pesach sets nothing, though Tu b'Av always falls on its weekday. He answers that the signs mark only what has already happened; Tu b'Av belongs to the future, to the 'day that is entirely Shabbos'. This is why the Gemara gives six reasons for Tu b'Av, none sufficient: the seventh will be known when Hashem makes a dance for the tzaddikim. He explains Tu b'Av as rejoicing that Jews merited to mourn, a sign of life, shown by the slain of Beitar who did not decay. Tu b'Av opens the days of teshuvah: each Jew resolves to be good, 'borrowing' from what he will become. Like David's watchmen awaiting morning, Jews keep hoping after every disappointment, a depth only a pointing finger can convey.

en: The atbash sign gives no day for the seventh of Pesach because Tu b'Av, which falls on its weekday, belongs to the future, and a sign cannot be made for what has not yet happened.
The Gemara's six reasons for Tu b'Av are each true but each insufficient, which itself shows that the real reason is still hidden until Moshiach comes.
On Tu b'Av Jews rejoice that they merited to mourn the Beis HaMikdash, a sign that they are alive and still hope for its rebuilding.
Tu b'Av is the first of the days of teshuvah, when each Jew resolves to improve and, like borrowed white garments, draws now on the good he will become.
A Jew never despairs: after every disappointed hope for Moshiach he hopes again, and this is the joy that will be revealed in the future.

title.en: Why the seventh of Pesach sets no day

summary.en: The Rav explains that Pesach, king of the festivals, sets the weekdays of the festivals by the atbash sign, and asks why the seventh day of Pesach, though Tu b'Av falls on its weekday, is not part of the sign. He answers that the sign marks only festivals already given; Tu b'Av belongs to the future, and its hint will be made when Moshiach comes.

title.en: Six reasons, and the missing seventh

summary.en: The Rav compares the Gemara's six reasons for Tu b'Av to a child who gives six excuses for coming late, since no one reason suffices. Each reason is true yet too small for the greatest festival; the seventh reason will be known when Hashem makes a dance for the tzaddikim and each will point with his finger.

title.en: Rejoicing that we mourned; the slain of Beitar

summary.en: The Rav explains Tu b'Av as the joy over having mourned the Beis HaMikdash for 1,912 years, a sign of the Jewish life force, 'rejoice with her all who mourn her'. He brings the slain of Beitar, who fought for Bar Koziva and whom the enemies wished to leave to rot, yet they did not decay: the hope for Moshiach is alive and does not decay.

title.en: A festival of the future; start of teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav ties Tu b'Av to the seventh day of Pesach, which points to the future redemption, and explains that it celebrates what will be. Tu b'Av opens the days of teshuvah: each Jew makes an accounting, adds Torah at night and takes on new resolutions, as a rav would say over farfel that what was until now is lost. Every Jew has his own redemption when he does teshuvah.

title.en: Borrowed white garments and endless hope

summary.en: The Rav explains that mitzvos are garments, like the soiled garments removed from Yehoshua the Kohen Gadol, and that on Tu b'Av a Jew 'borrows' white garments from the good he will become, bringing the Kotzker's remark about borrowing a father. He describes the disappointment when Moshiach did not come on Tisha b'Av, and brings 'watchmen for the morning': a Jew keeps hoping and rises from mourning to rejoice.

title.en: What only a finger can explain

summary.en: The Rav says all the disappointments will be sweetened into the great joy of the future Tu b'Av, the dance of the tzaddikim. Some ideas cannot be put into words and can only be pointed at with a finger; so too the depth of a Jewish heart that still hopes after 1,912 years, 'behold this is our G-d, we hoped for Him'. He closes with a blessing for the redemption.

catalogTitle: דברו על לב ירשלים - הרגשת ישראל בנחמת ציון

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Fifteenth of Av is the Yom Tov of the future redemption, felt in the heart of Klal Yisrael, the day Yirmiyahu of Tisha B'Av turns back into Shlomo HaMelech.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Mishnah at the end of Taanis and asks why it ends with Shlomo HaMelech, why the daughters danced in the vineyards, and why the Gemara needs six reasons for a day greater than Pesach. He asks why the Shulchan Aruch's calendar sign omits the seventh day of Pesach, and answers that it determines the Fifteenth of Av, a Yom Tov for a redemption that has not yet come. The six reasons are the reflected light of that future joy, the dance Hashem will make for the tzaddikim. Women grasp the redemption with feeling, so the daughters dance in the vineyards. He then sets Tisha B'Av against Shemini Atzeres and Yirmiyahu against Shlomo, quoting the Chasam Sofer that Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo. On the Fifteenth of Av one takes off Yirmiyahu's garments, adds in Torah, builds one's own Mikdash and rises from the grave of Tisha B'Av.

en: The seventh day of Pesach, the 'Shabbos' of Pesach, determines the weekday of the Fifteenth of Av, which is left out of the calendar sign because it celebrates a redemption still to come.
The Gemara's six reasons are true, but they are the reflected light of the real, seventh reason: the future dance Hashem will make for the tzaddikim.
Belief in the redemption comes from the heart and feeling, which is why the daughters, not the sons, go out to dance in the vineyards, the place of wine.
Tisha B'Av corresponds to Shemini Atzeres, and Yirmiyahu, the prophet of the destruction, is a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, whose day is Shemini Atzeres.
Every Jew has in him a Yirmiyahu and a Shlomo; on the Fifteenth of Av he should add in Torah, take on new resolutions and build his own Mikdash.
Shlomo conquered the whole world without war, through peace and Torah, and so he is the soul of the days of Moshiach.

title.en: The Mishnah's Fifteenth of Av and its puzzles

summary.en: The Rav reads the Mishnah at the end of Taanis about the daughters going out in borrowed white garments, ending with 'tze'enah ur'enah' and Shlomo HaMelech. He asks what Shlomo has to do with the Fifteenth of Av, why the Baraisa adds that they danced in the vineyards, and why the passuk speaks of daughters going to see the king.

title.en: Six reasons for one Yom Tov

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that asks what happened on the Fifteenth of Av and gives six reasons. He argues, with a mashal of a boy late to cheder, that many reasons weaken each other, and that reasons like the tribes intermarrying or the wood for the altar cannot explain a day greater than Pesach, Shavuos and Sukkos.

title.en: Why the seventh day of Pesach is missing

summary.en: The Rav explains the sign of the Shulchan Aruch by which each day of Pesach fixes the weekday of a later festival, since Pesach is the head of all festivals. He asks why the seventh day, the highest day of Pesach, is left out, when it would fix the Fifteenth of Av, both falling on Friday this year.

title.en: A Yom Tov for what is yet to come

summary.en: The Rav answers that the Fifteenth of Av follows Tisha B'Av, ending its seven days of mourning, and is fixed by the seventh day of Pesach, its Shabbos. The sign lists festivals for events that already happened, while the Fifteenth of Av celebrates the coming redemption, Nachamu, when a Jew should engrave in himself emunah in Moshiach.

title.en: The hidden seventh reason

summary.en: The Rav explains that every holy event casts its light before it happens, as Avraham ate matzos and wonders happened on Pesach night before the Exodus. The Gemara's six reasons are that reflected light; the seventh is Rabbi Elazar's teaching that Hashem will make a dance for the tzaddikim, which the daughters' dancing hints at.

title.en: Feeling and intellect: why the daughters dance

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gevuros Hashem that the matzos correspond to the Avos and the mind, the four cups of wine to the Imahos and feeling. He shows from Bnos Tzelofchad and from Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen that belief in the redemption is felt in the heart, and so the daughters dance in the vineyards, the place of wine.

title.en: Nachamu, Hashem comforts with the prophet

summary.en: The Rav brings the Pesikta that the people would accept comfort only from Hashem Himself, so Hashem goes with Yeshayahu into every shul on the seven Shabbosos of consolation. The seventh haftarah, 'sos asis', corresponds to the seventh of Pesach and speaks of chassan and kallah; the borrowed garments, as the Bnei Yissaschar says, are borrowed from the future.

title.en: Shemini Atzeres, the day of Shlomo

summary.en: The Rav sets Shemini Atzeres, the most joyful day, against Tisha B'Av, the saddest. He brings the Chasam Sofer that all festivals prepare for Shemini Atzeres, the haftarah of Shlomo completing the Beis HaMikdash, the Midrash that Shlomo was the fifteenth generation like the full moon, and Rebbe Reb Bunim that Shemini Atzeres is Shlomo's day.

title.en: Yirmiyahu, the prophet of Tisha B'Av

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yirmiyahu was born on Tisha B'Av, so 'cursed is the day I was born' states a fact. With the Midrash's mashal of a kohen who must disgrace his own mother, he describes Yirmiyahu's bitter lot, and contrasts it with Shlomo's era of peace, 'each man under his vine', against Yirmiyahu's 'no grapes on the vine'.

title.en: Yirmiyahu, a gilgul of Shlomo

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer that Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo: because Shlomo slept late on the day the Beis HaMikdash was dedicated, he had to return as Yirmiyahu and see its destruction. Hidden in Tisha B'Av lies the birth of Moshiach, and Yirmiyahu will yet bless the day he was born.

title.en: Eichah against Shir HaShirim

summary.en: The Rav notes twenty-two days in each of bein hametzarim and Rosh Hashanah to Shemini Atzeres, so Tisha B'Av corresponds to Shemini Atzeres. He pictures Yirmiyahu finishing Eichah and remembering that as Shlomo he wrote Shir HaShirim, and explains why, when Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos as this year, one eats 'like the meal of Shlomo in his time'.

title.en: The black background, from Yirmiyahu to Yeshayahu

summary.en: The Rav brings a Lubavitch teaching that the three weeks through Shemini Atzeres are like a colorful embroidery on a black background, and adds that the reading of Tisha B'Av already hints at 'atah hor'eisa' of the hakafos. From the Fifteenth of Av one exchanges Yirmiyahu's garments for Shlomo's crown, and Yeshayahu, the prophet of consolation, is the prophet of Shemini Atzeres.

title.en: Shlomo conquered the world with peace

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shlomo ruled the whole world without ever going to war, an 'ish menuchah', and is the soul of Moshiach. He tells that at the judgment of the two women no sword could be found among his soldiers, and one had to be brought from a museum, because Shlomo conquered with Torah.

title.en: Putting on Shlomo's garments; build your own Mikdash

summary.en: The Rav explains that on the Fifteenth of Av, after the seven days of mourning, Yirmiyahu turns into Shlomo, and the Mishnah's 'day of his wedding' and 'day of his heart's joy' mean taking on new Torah and building the Mikdash. Every Jew has a Yirmiyahu and a Shlomo, and he should build his own Mikdash, since what a Jew does Hashem does too; this is done through good middos.

title.en: Jews who are festivals

summary.en: The Rav explains why Tisha B'Av is called a mo'ed and that Jews themselves are mo'adim: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is Shabbos, a talmid chacham is Shabbos who gives to the weekday Jews, and there are Jews who are Yom Tov, Chol HaMoed, Pesach, Shavuos or Sukkos. He tells, as Tosafos brings, how the generation of the desert lay down in graves every Tisha B'Av until the fortieth year.

title.en: Reb Tisha B'Av, rise from the grave

summary.en: The Rav describes a gifted young man, 'Reb Tisha B'Av', who wastes his powers and lies in a grave. On the Fifteenth of Av, the start of preparation for the Days of Awe, one makes a cheshbon hanefesh, adds in Torah, leaves the grave and looks at the Torah, the 'eishes chayil'. He ends with a brachah for new luchos and to see Yirmiyahu in the garments of Shlomo.

catalogTitle: A Time for the Renewal of אמונה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Nisan, the month of HaChodesh hazeh lachem, is the birth of Klal Yisrael as a nation of believers, and therefore the time for every Jew to renew himself and his emunah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Nisan as a beginning: of the Mishkan's avodah and of Klal Yisrael as a nation bound by Torah. He asks why Rashi calls HaChodesh hazeh lachem the first mitzvah when milah and gid hanasheh came earlier, and turns to the mitzvah of emunah. A Jew believes by inheritance, as maaminim bnei maaminim, like the instinct passed down in a beaver or spider; Avraham Avinu was a new species that completed creation. A Jew who denies is sick, his heart clogged by aveiros and forbidden food. There is also emunah through examining nature and history. Following the Rambam in Yesodei HaTorah ch. 8, the Torah rests on what millions saw at Sinai, not on one man's wonders. That answers Rashi: milah is kept only because Moshe told it, so HaChodesh was the first mitzvah, and its nature is renewal. Nisan, the head of all moadim, is the time to renew one's emunah, with matzah as its food.

en: Nisan is a beginning in several ways: the Mishkan's avodah began then, and Klal Yisrael became a nation, a people defined only by the Torah.
Jews believe in Hashem by inheritance, as maaminim bnei maaminim, an instinct passed down from Avraham Avinu.
A Jew who says he does not believe has a sick emunah: aveiros, and above all forbidden food, clog the heart that believes by instinct.
Following the Rambam, the Rav explains that the Torah rests on the experience of millions at Har Sinai, not on the wonders of one man.
HaChodesh hazeh lachem is the first mitzvah because it was the first mitzvah Moshe Rabbeinu gave Klal Yisrael, and its essence is renewal.
Rosh Chodesh Nisan and Pesach are a time of teshuvah and renewal, when a Jew can become a new person and renew his emunah.
Matzah, which Chazal call food of emunah, strengthens the inborn emunah just as forbidden food weakens it.

title.en: Nisan as a beginning and Rashi's question

summary.en: The Rav describes Nisan as a beginning: of Birkas HaChamah, of the avodah in the Mishkan, and of Klal Yisrael as a nation bound only by Torah. He asks why Rashi calls HaChodesh hazeh lachem the first mitzvah when milah and gid hanasheh came earlier, and introduces the mitzvah of emunah, which the Rambam counts and the Ramban calls the foundation of all mitzvos.

title.en: Emunah by inheritance from Avraham

summary.en: The Rav asks how one can be commanded to believe and why Anochi Hashem is a statement rather than a command. He answers that Jews are maaminim bnei maaminim who believe by instinct, like a beaver building a dam or a spider spinning a web, and that Avraham Avinu was a new species whose arrival completed creation.

title.en: When emunah becomes sick

summary.en: The Rav compares a Jew who denies Hashem to a body whose natural hunger was spoiled by eating sawdust: his emunah is not missing but sick. Aveiros, and especially forbidden food, clog the heart, so one must be very careful with kashrus and seek a healer of the soul.

title.en: Emunah through examining the world

summary.en: The Rav describes a second kind of emunah, reached by examining nature, the human body and history. A wristwatch cannot assemble itself, so the claim that the universe came by itself is an excuse not to keep the Torah; he brings the Ramban that daily life is full of hidden miracles.

title.en: The mesorah of millions at Sinai

summary.en: Since emunah is a mitzvah it has halachos, and the Rambam teaches that it rests on mesorah. Other faiths followed one charismatic individual; the Torah was heard by millions at Har Sinai, and such a public event cannot be faked, just as no one can deny George Washington or Julius Caesar.

title.en: The Rambam: belief in Moshe from Sinai, not wonders

summary.en: The Rav says the other faiths also accept that the Torah was given at Sinai but watered it down, claiming Hashem changed His mind. He brings the Rambam in Yesodei HaTorah ch. 8 that Jews did not believe Moshe because of his wonders, which leave a doubt of magic, but because they themselves saw Hashem speak to him at Sinai.

title.en: Answering Rashi: the first mitzvah through Moshe

summary.en: Returning to Rashi, the Rav answers that milah is kept not because Avraham passed it down but because Moshe Rabbeinu told it, so HaChodesh hazeh lachem was the first mitzvah. Its very character is renewal: as a new moon appears in a dark sky, a new nation came out of the darkness of Mitzrayim.

title.en: Renew yourself: the fountain of youth

summary.en: The Rav teaches that the mitzvah of HaChodesh tells each Jew to renew himself, citing Rabbeinu Yonah that a baal teshuvah is a new person and the words of Kiddush Levanah. Every Rosh Chodesh, and more so Rosh Chodesh Nisan, is a time of teshuvah; the fountain of youth the nations searched for is HaChodesh hazeh lachem, a mikveh in which to take new resolutions.

title.en: Pesach, head of the moadim, and nature's renewal

summary.en: The Rav explains that Pesach is the head of all the moadim and the only one carrying kares, since its essence is a new bond with Hashem, the opposite of being cut off. Because the nation was renewed in Nisan, all of nature renews itself then, and a person should not be the exception.

title.en: Avraham's miracles and matzah, food of emunah

summary.en: The Rav notes that Avraham Avinu's miracles all happened on Pesach, since he was the first Jew. He concludes that one renews one's emunah through matzah, which Chazal call food of emunah, and that is why kosher matzah matters so much, and closes with a brachah for a Pesach of renewed emunah.

catalogTitle: זמן לשאוב יראת שמים בעד הכנה לר"ה' זמן של שידוכים' ז' ימים אחר היו"ט הגדול של ט' באב לעתיד.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Chamishah Asar b'Av as the start of the season of yiras shamayim and teshuvah leading to Yom Kippur, a day of shidduchim between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and the yom tov of the hidden good in the churban: that the avodah of Jews in galus is more precious to Hashem than ever, which is why one adds in Torah from that day.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with parshas Eikev and its haftarah as the week of yiras Hashem within the seven weeks of comfort, and with the tradition that the days of teshuvah begin on the fifteenth of Av. Using the Mishnah about the girls of Yerushalayim, he describes the day as a shidduch between Hashem and Klal Yisrael whose tenaim are the passuk of fearing and loving Hashem. A story about a man in Biala who chose his purchase right after Yom Kippur shows that a person's choice is good when he is free of sin, and the Rav explains that Yom Kippur's power already begins on Chamishah Asar b'Av. He then contrasts holy fear, which comes from wholeness, with fear born of lack. In the second part he explains, through the Pesikta on 'Sing, O barren one' and the words of the Arizal, the Chiddushei HaRim and the Chasam Sofer, that avodah in galus is more precious than in the times of the Beis Hamikdash. Chamishah Asar b'Av is the day to rejoice in this and to add in Torah.

en: Chamishah Asar b'Av is a time to draw yiras shamayim, falling in the week of parshas Eikev, the week of fear of Hashem among the seven weeks of comfort, and it opens the days of teshuvah.
The day of shidduchim is a shidduch between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and its tenaim are the passuk 'What does Hashem ask of you, but to fear Hashem… and to love Him'.
Yom Kippur makes a person free of sin, so his choice is good, and since the process of Yom Kippur begins on Chamishah Asar b'Av, that day too is a time when a Jew's choice is at its best.

Since the churban, the avodah of Jews in galus is more precious to Hashem than the avodah of the great tzaddikim of the Beis Hamikdash era, as the Pesikta teaches on 'the children of the desolate are more than the children of the married one'.

On Chamishah Asar b'Av, rising from the mourning of Tisha b'Av, one rejoices that our avodah is precious, makes a reckoning that the opportunity may end when Moshiach comes, and adds in Torah, tefillah and Yiddishkeit.

title.en: The week of yiras Hashem and the start of teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav presents parshas Eikev and its haftarah as the week of yiras Hashem among the seven weeks of comfort, recalls that Rebbe Reb Bunim learned Sefer Devarim as his mussar, and brings the tradition that the days of teshuvah begin on Chamishah Asar b'Av. He reads the Mishnah about the girls of Yerushalayim and calls the day a time to draw yiras shamayim.

title.en: A shidduch between Hashem and Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav describes the day of shidduchim as the time when Hashem chooses Klal Yisrael, who in galus say 'do not look at me for I am dark', and says the tenaim of this shidduch are the passuk of fearing and loving Hashem. He ends with a story of a Chernobyler tzaddik that the recording leaves mostly unclear.

title.en: Gap in the recording

summary.en: A long stretch with almost no transcribed speech.

title.en: Choosing right after Yom Kippur: the man from Biala

summary.en: The Rav notes that a person's match is announced from heaven but one must merit to receive it, and that matches were once chosen around Yom Kippur. He tells of a man in Biala who picked a sealed box right after Yom Kippur and always had the finest in town, explaining that free of sin, his choice was sure to be good.

title.en: Yom Kippur begins on Chamishah Asar b'Av

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yom Kippur is a day when a Jew's nature and choice incline to good, and that the avodah of teshuvah which ends on Yom Kippur begins on Chamishah Asar b'Av, so the end is already in the beginning. On this day a Jew's choice is at its best, and he applies 'u'vacharta ba'chaim' and the call to the young man to lift his eyes: to choose a path of Torah.

title.en: Av, Yerushalayim and a fear born of wholeness

summary.en: The Rav explains that Av and Yerushalayim, joy for the whole world in time and in place, became mourning with the churban, and that from Chamishah Asar b'Av the rebuilding begins. Yerushalayim is 'yirah shleimah': holy fear comes from wholeness, unlike ordinary fear, which comes from what a person lacks, as one fears a lion.

title.en: Why avodah in galus is so precious

summary.en: The Rav says the Gemara's reasons for Chamishah Asar b'Av hide a deep inner meaning, and that some of it may now be said as Moshiach approaches. Relying on the Chiddushei HaRim and the Pesikta on 'Sing, O barren one', and on the Arizal's words to R' Chaim Vital, he explains that the avodah of Jews in galus is more precious to Hashem than that of the giants of the Beis Hamikdash era.

title.en: The two sides of Tisha b'Av

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chiddushei HaRim, who rose from shivah for his brother on Chamishah Asar b'Av, and asks why the end of mourning should be a yom tov. He answers that Tisha b'Av holds two opposite things: the churban and hester panim, which grow each year, and the gain that our avodah is now more precious; but on Tisha b'Av one cannot rejoice in that gain, since the honor of Hashem requires the Beis Hamikdash.

title.en: Rejoicing and making a reckoning

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer that for ourselves galus is better, since in the days of Moshiach there is no difficulty in serving Hashem, and we pray for the Beis Hamikdash only for the honor of Heaven. Therefore, once the mourning ends, Chamishah Asar b'Av was set as a day to rejoice that we are precious to Hashem and to make a reckoning to grab more Torah and mitzvos now.

title.en: Adding in Torah from Chamishah Asar b'Av

summary.en: The Rav explains the Gemara's call to add in learning from Chamishah Asar b'Av: not because the nights grow longer, but because each year's new hester panim makes our avodah more precious, and Moshiach may come at any moment. One must always pray for the Beis Hamikdash, yet may make this reckoning and add in Torah, tefillah and every part of Yiddishkeit.

catalogTitle: לבנה בשלימותה - התגלות השכינה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the dor hamidbar knew on Tu b'Av that the decree had ended because only then could they sense the moon, the middas malchus and yiras shamayim, which had been hidden since the sin of the meraglim.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara's reason for the yom tov of Tu b'Av: every Tisha b'Av in the desert part of the generation died in graves they dug, and in the fortieth year they kept lying down night after night until the full moon of the fifteenth told them the decree was over. He asks how they could have doubted the date on the fourteenth, when the moon is almost full. He tells how the Radziner Rebbe brought his techeiles to the Sfas Emes, who said he did not smell techeiles. Through the Ramchal's question on the berachah of Yotzer and the Divrei Yoel on Rabbeinu Tam, he develops an upper and a lower sun and moon. The moon is malchus and yiras shamayim, which is the sense of smell; after the meraglim it was hidden, and on Tu b'Av, the start of the awakening toward Rosh Hashanah, they sensed it again.

en: In the fortieth year the dor hamidbar lay down in their graves night after night, and only the full moon of the fifteenth of Av showed them the decree was over, so they made a yom tov.
There is an upper sun and moon and a lower sun and moon; the visible sun's power to sustain the world comes down from the upper sun each dawn through the tzimtzumim.
The moon is middas malchus, which is yiras shamayim, and yiras shamayim is the sense of smell; therefore the moon is called yareach, from rei'ach, smell.
Since the sin of the meraglim there was hester panim: the physical moon was there, but the moon one can 'smell' was hidden.
Tu b'Av is when the awakening toward Rosh Hashanah begins, and on it the dor hamidbar sensed the moon, middas malchus, revealed again.

title.en: Why Tu b'Av is a yom tov

summary.en: After opening singing, the Rav brings the Gemara's reason for Tu b'Av: each Tisha b'Av in the desert part of the generation died in graves they had dug, and in the fortieth year they lay down night after night until the full moon of the fifteenth showed them the decree was over.

title.en: A question, and the Radziner's techeiles

summary.en: The Rav asks how they could have thought they miscounted on the fourteenth, when the moon is nearly full. He then tells how the Radziner Rebbe found the chilazon, made techeiles and argued for it, and how the Sfas Emes held it to his nose and said he did not smell techeiles.

title.en: The upper sun and the lower sun

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramchal's question on the berachah of Yotzer, which speaks of opening the gates of the east each day, and his answer that the influence of an upper sun comes down each dawn into the visible sun. He adds the Divrei Yoel, who answers the Baal HaTanya's objection to Rabbeinu Tam's 72 minutes with the upper sun.

title.en: The moon, malchus and the sense of smell

summary.en: The Rav explains that the moon is malchus and yiras shamayim, which is smell, so the Sfas Emes meant the techeiles lacked yiras shamayim, as there will be no techeiles until Moshiach. The moon is hidden on Rosh Hashanah until Jews crown Hashem with the shofar, and after the meraglim the 'smelled' moon was hidden altogether.

title.en: Sensing the moon on Tu b'Av

summary.en: The Rav answers his question: they thought a merit was holding off the decree day after day, as with the sotah, until on Tu b'Av they sensed the moon and malchus. Tu b'Av is when the awakening toward Rosh Hashanah and teshuvah begins, and it brings lights of geulah.

title.en: Singing

summary.en: Almost no transcribed speech from here to the end: a stretch of lost audio, then singing, apparently including the words of Mimkomcha.

oneLiner.en: Opening the sixth perek of Pirkei Avos, the Rav explains that the chachamim who learn Torah lishmah become one with the Torah, so that even their names and their ordinary words carry holiness.

abstract.en: The Rav begins with the sixth perek of Avos, a baraisa added to the five perakim and learned before Shavuos, a time when a Jew can always begin anew. He asks why the baraisa names the chachamim when there is no dispute, and answers that one who learns Torah lishmah unites with the Torah, like meat in a fire that becomes fire, so his very name is Torah. Mentioning a holy name draws down kedushah, as with Chevron in the Beis Hamikdash and Eretz Yisrael in Moshe's words. The word 'mishnah' suggests doubling: tzaddikim speak to people while addressing Hashem, as David did with Naval, illustrated by stories of tzaddikim. Turning to Torah lishmah, he explains that the same Torah is received through each person's middah, discusses lishmah and shelo lishmah, and ends with how refined things, like wine for Kiddush and Olam Haba, are the most easily affected.

en: The sixth perek of Avos is a baraisa added to the five perakim in the style of the Mishnah, and it is learned at the time of Shavuos.
The Rav says a Jew must always be able to lift himself up and begin a new account, without being held back by his past.
The names of the chachamim are themselves Torah, because one who learns lishmah becomes united with the Torah.
Mentioning a holy name, of a tzaddik, of Chevron or of Eretz Yisrael, draws down kedushah and salvation.
Tzaddikim can say one thing with several meanings, speaking to people while really addressing the Ribono shel Olam.
Each person receives the same Torah according to his own middah and level, and learns lishmah as far as his level allows.
The more refined a thing is, the more easily it is affected, as with wine for Kiddush and with Olam Haba.
