the sigh of a simple Jew

title.en: The hardest end of the Egyptian exile

summary.en: The Rav says he will repeat well-known things that need constant reminding, as the Mesilas Yesharim says. Following Reb Elchonon Wasserman he presents the exile in Egypt as a model of today's exile, whose final stage, just as Moshe announced the redemption, was the hardest, culminating in Pharaoh's 'tichbad ha'avodah'.

title.en: Pharaoh's aim: no time to think

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that the Jews gathered on Shabbos to read scrolls handed down from Yaakov and Yosef promising redemption, and Pharaoh took even that day away. With the Mesilas Yesharim he explains that the tactic is to leave no moment of calm, and says today too there is a klipah of 'tichbad ha'avodah' that leaves no time for yishuv hadaas.

title.en: A house of slaves and the precious sigh

summary.en: The Rav explains 'mibeis avadim' as Egypt's culture of work without thought, and calls America in particular such a house. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching, via the Magen Avraham, that Pharaoh feared even the sigh of a simple, worn-out Jew who runs to daven Minchah, and the story of the Ba'al HaTanya asking his jailer 'ayeka', where are you in the world.

title.en: Forced labor then, chosen burden now

summary.en: The Rav describes the poverty of Jews in Europe, who worked sixteen hours a day for black bread, and whose sigh was precious; in America one who draws the klipah onto himself by choice is at fault and loses Heaven's help. He adds that the sitra achra invents new forms of 'tichbad ha'avodah', so that the time saved by inventions is filled with new burdens.

title.en: From the drugstore phone to the cell phone

summary.en: The Rav recalls when a phone call meant a nickel in a drugstore booth, and how he himself had no phone until a break-in at night. Once everyone has a phone, he says, people are busy with it all day, and now cell phones make them walk around like zombies; he grants a businessman's need and judges a kollel yungerman favorably, but an always-on cell phone without need draws the klipah and takes away the last moment of peace.

title.en: Phones in the beis medrash

summary.en: The Rav tells of a man who objected to the sign banning cell phones in the beis medrash because of business emergencies, and explains that a ringing phone brings lightness into learning and davening. He brings a writing of the Lubavitcher Rebbe that a seder of learning should be like Shabbos, and reads 'melech l'sadeh ne'evad' as the king who is really a slave to his field.

title.en: Social pressure: kiddushes, sheva brachos, weddings

summary.en: The Rav lists the social culture of having to attend every aufruf, bar mitzvah, vort and several kiddushes after davening, and the new custom of sheva brachos every night, bringing a story of the Skverer Rebbe to ask whether everything Rebbes do must be imitated. He recalls the simple delicatessen at his own wedding, says lavish weddings leave people in debt for life, and calls these pressures part of the klipah of 'tichbad ha'avodah'.

title.en: Going out of this Egypt

summary.en: The Rav calls on everyone to leave this Egypt, gaining time to learn, daven and bring joy into the home, and notes that the pressure causes tension and even depression. He asks that each decision to buy something be weighed against this klipah, says one who frees himself is given calm and joy from Heaven, and closes with the season after Chamisha Asar b'Shevat and the parshiyos of the Exodus.

catalogTitle: פרישות מתאוות: בפרט מתאוות דעיקבתא דמשיחא.

oneLiner.en: At a seudas Rosh Chodesh Adar, the Rav teaches that every person needs pleasure, and a Jew should draw it from Torah, tefillah and avodas Hashem rather than chase the new pleasures the world keeps inventing.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with two neglected one-line simanim in Shulchan Aruch, melaveh malkah and the seudah of Rosh Chodesh, and explains the Rosh Chodesh meal as a korban-like feast for the diminished moon and a seudah of Moshiach, tied to malchus beis Dovid and to Shaul's anger at Dovid's family feast. Adar has strong mazal, and Jews sit at this seudah even in a time when the sitra achra rules. Building on Dovid's words 'all my wellsprings are in You', he brings a psychologist's rule that a person must have pleasure, and shows from the Yismach Moshe and Rabbi Aharon of Karlin that tzaddikim had it from Torah and tefillah. The danger is drawing in new taavos, new foods and goyish joys. He then praises the miracle that avodas Hashem survives in galus, including in his own beis medrash, and closes with the Yaaros Devash, whose pleasure was standing in tefillah, and a call to begin Adar with simcha.

en: The seudah of Rosh Chodesh is like a korban for the diminished moon, and a seudah of Moshiach bound up with malchus beis Dovid.
Hashem created man so that he must have pleasure; without any enjoyment a person breaks down.
Tzaddikim who tasted nothing in food had the greatest pleasure, from Torah, tefillah and Tehillim.
The bodily pleasures a person was created with are his test, but drawing in new pleasures and new foods distances him from Hashem.
A Jew must not let goyish joys into his home, even a little, as with chametz.
The survival of avodas Hashem in galus is an even greater miracle than the survival of the Jews themselves.
A Jew should take his pleasure from what Hashem provides, Torah, mitzvos and tefillah, and begin Adar with that simcha.

candidateTopics: miracle of jewish survival in galus

title.en: The neglected seudah of Rosh Chodesh

summary.en: The Rav notes two simanim in Shulchan Aruch, melaveh malkah and the seudah of Rosh Chodesh, that people do not keep, and tells of a Yerushalmi who left his rental income for Rosh Chodesh meals. He explains the meal as a korban for the diminished moon and a seudah of Moshiach, and shows this in Shaul's anger at Dovid's Rosh Chodesh family feast.

title.en: Adar's strong mazal and 'all my wellsprings'

summary.en: The Rav marvels that Jews sit at a Rosh Chodesh seudah while the sitra achra rules, and explains that Adar's mazal is strong, bringing the Gemara that a Jew should push off a case against a gentile to Adar. Adar is a time of ratzon, and he introduces Dovid's words 'all my wellsprings are in You', warning that he will speak sharply and is speaking to himself.

title.en: Man must have pleasure, and tzaddikim had theirs

summary.en: The Rav brings a psychologist's rule that a person fed only through a tube will break down, because Hashem made man to need pleasure. He asks how the Yismach Moshe, who once ate soap water as his supper unawares, fits this, and answers that he had the greatest pleasure from Gemara, tefillah and Tehillim, adding a story of Rabbi Aharon of Karlin and a vort of the Kotzker.

title.en: Natural tests versus new taavos

summary.en: The Rav explains that bodily pleasures are a person's given test, and holding back from sin is itself kedushah, while one can also enjoy learning. But one who seeks out new pleasures, like lying in a newly bought tub, cannot at the same time feel the joy of a blatt Gemara or Shabbos; Hashem can forgive the natural taavos, but drawing in new ones is far away.

title.en: Joy in avodas Hashem and the new foods

summary.en: From the seder's request to rejoice in Hashem's service, the Rav says every yungerman knows moments of great pleasure in avodas Hashem, on Shabbos, Yom Tov, at the Megillah, Akdamus or in the sukkah, despite times of dullness. Running after the world's new foods, a new cake at every kiddush, distances a person from Hashem and from 'all my wellsprings are in You'.

title.en: Pleasure from Torah, not the spider's web

summary.en: The Rav sums up that one should enjoy what Hashem provides, not what the sitra achra offers, reading the Mishnah 'one who enjoys words of Torah' as meaning he no longer draws vitality from the world. The new inventions are a web that traps a person like a fly, so one must hold back from new tests; he applies 'do not rejoice, Yisrael, like the nations' and contrasts a Jewish piece of kugel with goyish pleasures.

title.en: Not even a trace, and the miracle of survival

summary.en: The Rav says he painted it in vivid colors, but even a trace of goyish joy must be kept out like chametz; the beis medrash itself filters out those with no connection to avodas Hashem. He then turns to the miracle of Jewish survival in galus, bringing the Yaavetz's count of the vanished empires, and mentions Paras, which never harmed the Jews.

title.en: The greater miracle: avodas Hashem in galus

summary.en: The Rav says Jewish survival in galus is a greater miracle than Yetzias Mitzrayim, only hidden in nature like the Megillah, and the survival of avodas Hashem greater still, though the Nazi aimed at the Talmud and today's yeshivos hold more students than all prewar ones. He calls his own chevra Emunas Yisroel one of the great miracles and ties it to the seudas Rosh Chodesh, where the moon that died rises again.

title.en: Gan Eden or Gehinnom in the same davening

summary.en: The Rav laments those who do not take advantage of the beis medrash's davening, especially on weekdays, and brings the Gemara that Gan Eden and Gehinnom are one place: the same davening is Gan Eden for one and Gehinnom for another. Other shuls draw people with bagels and lox; theirs serves Nishmas and Shabbos tefillos, and a person should enjoy Hashem's recipe, not foreign foods.

title.en: The Yaaros Devash's pleasure in tefillah

summary.en: The Rav brings Rabbi Aharon's saying that he does not trust a bochur until he sees him as a yungerman, and urges continuing. He reads a letter of the Yaaros Devash about his long kavanos in tefillah, for which people laughed at him, and his answer that standing before Hashem in tefillah is his portion. He closes that Rosh Chodesh Adar is a time to begin with the simcha of Torah, mitzvos and tefillah, with a brachah.

catalogTitle: פרקי אבות פרק ששי: “זוכה לדברים הרבה” - תורה היא מועט המחזיק את המרובה. “נקרא רע” - קשר בינו ובין ה'. “אוהב את המקום' אוהב את הבריות.”

oneLiner.en: On the Mishnah in Avos 6:1, the Rav explains that Torah is the small thing that holds the many, that the whole world exists to serve the tzaddik who learns Torah lishmah, and that through Torah he becomes a friend bound to Hashem and a lover of Hashem and of every Jew.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with 'he merits many things' and explains that the root of everything is a small point that contains the many: Rosh Hashanah for the year, the place of the Mikdash for the world, and above all the Torah, which is our Mikdash. A child and the greatest gedolim learn the same Chumash, yet each sees more. One who learns lishmah becomes part of Torah, and his words too contain much. He then explains that the whole world was created only to serve such a tzaddik, with the Ba'al Shem Tov's story of the collapsing building, Ben Zoma, the nations in Avodah Zarah and a merchant's mashal. From the Maharal on the Torah beginning with a beis he shows that Torah turns curse into blessing, and that with emunah nothing bad exists. Finally he explains 'rei'a' and 'ohev', the union of the tzaddik with Hashem, and why loving a Jew is loving Hashem.

en: The root of every realm is a small point that contains the many, and the root of all roots, of places and of times, is the Torah.
Unlike worldly wisdom, which holds no more than the paper it is written on, the same Chumash and Gemara a small child learns hold what the greatest gedolim see in them.
One who learns Torah lishmah becomes a real part of Torah, so his own words too become 'many things' that contain much.
The whole world, including the nations in exile, exists only to serve the tzaddik who learns Torah lishmah, whether they know it or not.
Torah turns curse into blessing; for one with full emunah everything Hashem does is good, and nothing bad exists for him.
Through Torah the one who learns becomes united with Hashem, so he is called both 'rei'a' and 'ohev', and loving every Jew follows from loving Hashem.

the world created for the tzaddik
union of the tzaddik with Hashem

title.en: Torah: the small that holds the many

summary.en: The Rav explains 'he merits many things' through the idea that the root of each realm is a small point holding the many: Rosh Hashanah for the year, the Mikdash for the world, Eretz Yisroel, and above all the Torah. He contrasts worldly wisdom, which holds no more than its paper, with the Chumash a child learns and the gedolim see more in.

title.en: Becoming part of Torah; learning as a korban

summary.en: The Rav explains that one who learns lishmah becomes part of Torah, bringing the Gemara of Moshe Rabbeinu and Rabbi Akiva, and shows how one word yields many. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar that learning the parsha of korbanos earns the reward of the larger korban, and tells how Rabbi Elchonon Wasserman answered a man who had not seen the reward the Gemara promises for Kiddush.

title.en: The whole world is worthwhile for him

summary.en: On 'the whole world is worthwhile for him' the Rav brings the Gemara in Berachos, the Ba'al Shem Tov's story of a great building that stood only to shelter a tzaddik from rain, and Ben Zoma's blessing on the crowds. Like the limbs of a body, every part of creation serves the tzaddik, even the nations in exile, as a teacher serves a king's son.

title.en: The nations' roads were made for Yisroel

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Avodah Zarah where the nations will claim they built markets and roads for Yisroel, and explains that in truth every road, invention and telephone exists for the sake of a Jew's learning or mitzvah, though the builders meant only their own needs.

title.en: The merchant's ships: why it is worth it

summary.en: The Rav asks how it can be worth creating a world where the wicked outnumber the tzaddikim, and answers with a mashal of a merchant who sends twenty ships knowing nineteen will sink, since one ship's profit covers all. So too the tikkun one tzaddik brings outweighs the loss of many reshaim.

title.en: Torah begins with a beis, above the world

summary.en: The Rav brings the Maharal that Torah is above the world: creation starts with a beis while the Aseres HaDibros start with an aleph, and in Tehillim 19 Torah is the eighth passuk after seven about creation. He then brings the Midrash that beis stands for berachah, and explains that where Torah is, even the aleph of curse turns into blessing.

title.en: Ha'azinu, emunah, and nothing is bad

summary.en: The Rav asks why the parshiyos of Ha'azinu do not end on a good word, and answers that Ha'azinu is the foundation of emunah, and with emunah nothing bad exists. He tells of Reb Zusha, who told the Maggid's visitor that nothing bad had ever happened to him, and explains that at Matan Torah, with 'Anochi', even the bitter is sweetened and turns to good, like the chametz of the Shavuos loaves.

title.en: Rei'a and ohev: union through Torah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Maharal's distinction that friendship (rei'a) is mutual while love (ohev) can be one-sided, and explains that the one who learns lishmah merits both because Torah, Hashem's own wisdom, binds the upper and lower worlds into one. He brings the Midrash that in the future 'kadosh' will be said before tzaddikim, which will then be understood as Hashem's own honor.

title.en: Shlomo on Hashem's throne; Hashem revealed through the tzaddik

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shlomo HaMelech sat 'on Hashem's throne' because in him people saw Hashem's kingship, and brings the Midrash that one who serves Hashem becomes like Him, as tzaddikim also revived the dead. Hashem is revealed through the tzaddik, so he is a friend bound to Hashem and loved by Hashem and by Yisroel, and he loves Hashem and people.

title.en: Two friends in Rome; loving a Jew is loving Hashem

summary.en: The Rav tells a story brought by a commentator on 'love your fellow as yourself, I am Hashem': two friends in Rome each wanted to be hanged in the other's place, and the king asked to join their friendship. He explains that one loves a Jew because of his G-dly portion, so the two mitzvos of love are one, and that the higher a person rises, the more he is bound to other Jews.

catalogTitle: מעשה ברבי אליעזר וכו - What our Sages Accomplished in בני ברק

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the descendants of Haman who learned Torah in Bnei Brak carried a hidden holy point from Timna, and that the Tannaim came to Bnei Brak on Pesach to lift them to the level of Krias Shema.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a sefer's words that on Pesach a Jew can leave his straits not step by step. He then asks how descendants of Haman could learn Torah in Bnei Brak, when Hashem swore no converts would come from Amalek. His answer runs through Timna: she longed to cling to Avraham's family, and as a mere pilegesh to Eliphaz her holy point never merged with Amalek. Bringing the Kedushas Levi, he explains that Esther's seudah, prepared from Pesach food, drew Haman briefly out of tumah, and suggests that Zeresh, who escaped, carried that spark to the forebears of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas. Haman's descendants could not say Krias Shema of Shacharis, because of Zeresh's advice to hang Mordechai at daybreak. The Tannaim therefore came to Bnei Brak on Pesach and lifted Timna's children to Shema Yisrael. He closes with the father's descent to his children on Seder night.

en: The Rav quotes a sefer that on Pesach a Jew can leave his straits all at once, not step by step as at other times.
Timna's longing to join Avraham's family was never lost; because she was only a pilegesh, her point stayed separate from Esav's and Amalek's seed.
That separate holy point is what allowed descendants of Haman to convert and learn Torah in Bnei Brak, among them Rav Shmuel bar Shilas.
Esther's seudah, made from Pesach food, brought Haman to the border of kedusha and roused in him the point from which Rav Shmuel bar Shilas would come.
Haman's descendants could not say Krias Shema of Shacharis, a trait from Zeresh's advice to hang Mordechai at daybreak; the Tannaim came to Bnei Brak on Pesach to lift them out of it.
On Seder night a father must go down from his highest levels and tell his young children the story of Yetzias Mitzrayim.

descendants of Haman who learned Torah in Bnei Brak
Maaseh b'Rabbi Eliezer in Bnei Brak
telling children Yetzias Mitzrayim on Seder night

title.en: Timna and the descendants of Haman in Bnei Brak

summary.en: After opening with a sefer's words that on Pesach one can leave his straits all at once, the Rav brings the Gemara about Menashe mocking the passuk of Timna and the Gemara that Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak. He asks how this fits with the Midrash that no converts are accepted from Amalek.

title.en: Timna's longing and the pilegesh who stays apart

summary.en: The Rav explains that a real longing shows a connection and is never lost, and that the first point of a thing endures even when hidden. Since Timna was only a pilegesh, who keeps her own identity unlike a wife, her point of longing for Avraham's seed stayed separate from Esav's seed and came out in Haman's descendants in Bnei Brak.

title.en: Haman's simcha and the escape of Zeresh

summary.en: The Rav brings the Kedushas Levi's question how Haman could leave Esther's seudah happy when simcha exists only in kedusha: the seudah drew him out of tumah to the border of kedusha, leaving him no source of life. Comparing this to Agag, he suggests that Zeresh, who escaped, carried from that night the spark of Timna that later surfaced in Haman's descendants in Bnei Brak.

title.en: Ad d'lo yada: giving life to the holy spark

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ari HaKadosh's explanation of drinking until one does not know between cursed Haman and blessed Mordechai: a blessing on Haman said in drunkenness gives life to the holy point in him without feeding his klipah. He adds that a Jew who blesses Zeresh, perhaps Shilas the mother of Rav Shmuel, helps bring forth such a child.

title.en: Esther's Pesach seudah and Rav Shmuel bar Shilas

summary.en: The Rav notes that Rav Shmuel bar Shilas is the source of the teaching that when Adar enters one increases simcha. Esther's seudah was made from the Pesach food she had prepared and not eaten during the fast, and Achashverosh loved such food; that kedusha gave Haman his simcha and roused the point of Rav Shmuel bar Shilas, so that his descendant taught the law of simcha.

title.en: Why Haman's descendants could not say Krias Shema

summary.en: The Rav suggests that Haman's descendants in Bnei Brak could not say Krias Shema of Shacharis, comparing it to people who tell him they cannot say Krias Shema from overconcentration. He traces it to the Midrash on Zeresh's advice to hang Mordechai at daybreak, to stop his Krias Shema, and repeats that on Pesach a Jew can leap out of tumah.

title.en: The Tannaim come to Bnei Brak on Pesach

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Tannaim chose Pesach to come to Bnei Brak and tell of Yetzias Mitzrayim, intending to benefit the souls of Haman's descendants and break Zeresh's klipah. He brings a sefer that mentioning Yetzias Mitzrayim relieves distress, and the Rambam in Perek Chelek that Shema Yisrael and 'va'achos Lotan Timna' are equally Torah.

title.en: From Timna to Shema; going down to the children

summary.en: The Rav concludes that the Tannaim lifted the children of Timna, the 'lowest' passuk, to the level of saying Krias Shema, with the power of Pesach. He describes the holiness of Seder night and says that the Torah asks a great man to go down from his heights to tell his small children of Yetzias Mitzrayim, joining 'va'achos Lotan Timna' to Shema Yisrael.

catalogTitle: פרקי אבות פרק ששי: תורה - מגלה סודות ללומד תורה לשמה' ת"ח משמח המקום והבריות' מלבשתו ענוה' ומרחקתו מן החטא' תורה מביא לומדיה לתיקונם' תורה למעלה מעוה"ז

oneLiner.en: Going through the praises of one who learns Torah lishmah in Avos chapter six, the Rav explains that Torah lifts a person above this world, to the 'eighth' level of yovel, Binah and neder, which frees him from sin and from his troubles.

abstract.en: The Rav reads the mishnah of Torah lishmah phrase by phrase. Learning lishmah uncovers the love of Hashem hidden in every Jew and brings love of Jews; the world is sustained in the merit of tzaddikim; Torah clothes a person in humility. Torah keeps him from sin: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey would not eat untithed food, and the Yeshuos Yaakov sensed a cake was not kosher. It brings him to his purpose and to the tikkun of his soul, so he need not return in another gilgul. From the Maharal on Tehillim 19 he develops that Torah belongs to the 'eighth', above the seven days of nature: Shavuos, the soul, yovel, which Sha'arei Orah identifies with Binah, Yom Kippur, the shofar, milah and neder. With the Ramban on neder and shevuah, the neder against the Canaanite king, and the daily checking of tzitzis, he shows how a Jew connects to that higher world when tefillah alone does not break through.

en: Every Jew has a natural love for Hashem that is only covered over, and learning Torah lishmah uncovers it; love of Jews follows, and is a measure of one's love of Hashem.
Torah keeps its learner from sin to the point that even his possessions, as an extension of his soul, are guarded, as with Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey.
A person was sent into the world on a mission to serve Hashem and rectify his soul; Torah keeps him aware of that purpose so he need not come back in another gilgul.
Torah belongs to the 'eighth', a world above the seven days of creation, which is why it is the eighth verse of Tehillim 19 and why Shavuos, the soul and yovel all share this level.
Yovel, the root of every Jewish soul, guarantees that no Jew is lost: even one sold to idolatry must be redeemed and return to his root.

A neder reaches higher than a shevuah: a shevuah is 'by Hashem' within the seven of this world, while a neder is 'to Hashem', to Binah above it, so a neder, the shofar and tzitzis can bring salvation where tefillah does not reach.

candidateTopics: love of Hashem and love of Jews

title.en: Torah lishmah: loving Hashem and His creatures

summary.en: The Rav opens the mishnah of one who learns Torah lishmah and the passuk that all a man's wealth is nothing against love. He explains that every Jew's love of Hashem is only covered, Torah uncovers it, and love of Jews is the measure of love of Hashem.

title.en: The world is sustained by tzaddikim; humility as a garment

summary.en: The Rav shows from Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa and from Adam's task in Gan Eden that the whole world's blessing comes through Jews who learn and serve Hashem, as man is the soul of the world. He then explains that Torah 'clothes' its learner in humility, since true anavah is too lofty to be reached by effort alone.

title.en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey

summary.en: On 'it distances him from sin' the Rav brings the Gemara of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey that would not eat untithed food, and explains with the Ba'al Shem Tov that a person's food and possessions are part of him and come to him by hashgachah pratis to be rectified, so his holiness extends to them.

title.en: The Yeshuos Yaakov's cake; Torah guards its learner

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Yeshuos Yaakov avoided a cake that turned out not to be kosher, and explains that Heaven guards one who learns lishmah. Like the eishes chayil who protects her husband, Torah guards its learner, as Dovid HaMelech said his feet led him to the beis medrash.

title.en: Sent to the world on a mission: 'Ayekah'

summary.en: On 'it brings him close to merit' the Rav explains that a person comes into the world on a shlichus, and tells how the Ba'al HaTanya explained Hashem's question to Adam, 'Where are you?', as a question to every person about his place in the world. Torah keeps a person mindful that he is only a guest here, and shows each one his own path.

title.en: Torah brings the tikkun of the soul

summary.en: The Rav asks why Elimelech was punished for leaving Eretz Yisrael and answers that his tikkun could have come through Torah. With the Maharal on Tehillim 19 he shows that Torah, the eighth verse, is above nature and 'restores the soul', and with the Bnei Yissaschar that whoever has not fulfilled all the mitzvos must return.

title.en: Sefirah, Shavuos and the eighth world

summary.en: The Rav calls this world a fair where one buys what to take back to the World to Come, and explains that some mitzvos and times draw the 'eighth world' above creation down here. Torah is one of them, which is why Tehillim 119 runs through the alef-beis eight times, and Shavuos, after seven weeks of refining the middos, brings heaven down to earth.

title.en: The soul's root: yovel and Binah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the soul comes from the eighth world, and from the haftarah's 'by the yuval it sends its roots' that yovel means the source. Torah is the root of yovel and of freedom; Sha'arei Orah calls Binah yovel, and in the yovel year each one returns to his field in Eretz Yisrael, his root.

title.en: No Jew is lost: sold to an idol

summary.en: From the passuk of a Jew sold to the 'eiker' of a stranger's family, which Rashi explains as sold to idolatry itself, the Rav teaches that even a soul sold to the Satan is sold only until yovel. Hashem will not let it remain there; idolatry will have to give up every Jewish soul it swallowed, and it must be redeemed.

title.en: Yovel's names: geulah, Kippurim, shofar, neder

summary.en: Following Sha'arei Orah, the Rav explains yovel's names: geulah (the Exodus, mentioned fifty times), Kippurim (Yom Kippur, when Jews live like the World to Come), the shofar that breaks the harsh judgment of Rosh Hashanah, and milah and healing on the eighth. Its last name is neder, which lifts a person above his troubles, as Yaakov vowed in his distress, and Kol Nidrei readies a person to connect to Yom Kippur.

title.en: The Ramban on neder and shevuah; tzitzis

summary.en: The Rav reads the Ramban in Parshas Matos: a shevuah is 'by Hashem' and a neder 'to Hashem', because shevuah comes from sheva, the seven of this world, while a neder reaches Binah, above it. He adds that tzitzis, the part of the garment that does not warm, reminds a person of what is above nature, and that such things free him from troubles where tefillah does not help.

title.en: The neder against the Canaanite; checking tzitzis

summary.en: The Rav explains why Parshas Matos, with the laws of nedarim, is read in the Three Weeks, and why Jews made a neder only in the war with the Canaanite king, when tefillah could not help. He then answers why the poskim say to check one's tzitzis every morning: before the battle of davening one connects to the eighth through their eight threads, and tzitzis is tied to geulah, as the Gemara in Berachos shows.

catalogTitle: הספד: על אדמו"ר מסאטמאר זצ"ל

oneLiner.en: Before Rosh Hashanah, the Rav speaks about the Satmar Rav after his passing, explaining that a tzaddik whose Torah is still learned and whose path is still followed has not truly departed, and describing his holiness, prayer, Torah and his battle for a pure belief in Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with 'Atem nitzavim hayom', Rosh Hashanah as the judgment of every day of the year, and the losses of the year, the last of them the passing of the Satmar Rav. He chooses not to give a hesped but to speak about the tzaddik, since speaking of a tzaddik draws holiness. From the Midrash that 'every illness and every plague not written in the Torah' is the death of tzaddikim, he explains that this curse exists only in the Oral Torah and cannot be reversed, unless the tzaddik's wisdom is not lost. Through Eliyahu, Elisha and a sefer of the Satmar Rav he concludes that learning a tzaddik's Torah keeps him alive. He then describes the Satmar Rav's Torah, kedushas habris, his krias haTorah, Megillah, Ahavah Rabbah, Shabbos and Yom Tov, tzedakah, his last instruction about kohanim, and compares him to Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai and Chizkiyahu in his fight for a pure geulah. He closes with the orphaned generation and the call to hold to the tzaddikim's mesorah.

en: Rosh Hashanah judges every day of the coming year, which is why it is called 'hayom'.
The Rav does not give a hesped but speaks of the tzaddik, because speech draws down what is spoken, and speaking of a tzaddik draws kedushah and taharah.
The death of tzaddikim, a curse hidden in 'every illness not written', is only the loss of the tzaddik's wisdom; where his Torah is learned, he is not truly gone.
The Rav describes the Satmar Rav's holiness, his Torah lishmah, his prayer and the way Shabbos and Yom Tov showed on his face.
Like Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai, the Satmar Rav fought for a pure geulah, and according to the Rav, those who still believe in Moshiach's coming owe it to him.
The generation is left orphaned, but for those who hold to the tzaddikim's mesorah and learn their Torah, the tzaddikim have not passed away.

candidateTopics: learning a tzaddik's Torah after his passing
belief in the coming of Moshiach

title.en: Atem nitzavim and a year of losses

summary.en: The Rav opens with 'Atem nitzavim hayom': Rosh Hashanah judges every day of the year. Had one known in Elul what this year would bring, one would have prayed harder; the gedolim were taken one after another, last of all the Satmar Rav, and he mentions the great mitzvah of a hesped.

title.en: Not a hesped, but speaking of the tzaddik

summary.en: Following those who for certain reasons do not say hespeidim, the Rav will only speak of the tzaddik: speech has the power to draw down, as with hekdesh and terumah, so one speaks only good. He brings the Chasam Sofer on the Gemara 'be warm at my hesped, for I will be standing there': the departed speaks through the speaker.

title.en: Death of tzaddikim, and why Ki Savo says 'arur'

summary.en: Nitzavim comforts after the curses of Ki Savo, and a Midrash reads 'every illness and every plague not written' as the death of tzaddikim. The Rav recalls asking his young cheder pupils why the Torah writes only 'arur' when Rashi says 'baruch' was also said; a child answered that Hashem left the blessing for the Oral Torah, which he supports with the Gemara on Chulda's mercy.

title.en: The one curse the Oral Torah cannot reverse

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar: Rabbi Yossi asked why Ki Savo has no consolation, and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai answered, from Eliyahu, that its curses are all blessings and are meant for the nations. The Oral Torah turns the curses around, but the death of tzaddikim is not written at all; it exists only in the Oral Torah, so nothing can reverse it, unless the tzaddikim are not truly gone.

title.en: Eliyahu, Elisha and learning the tzaddik's Torah

summary.en: From Rashi on the passing of Eliyahu, the Rav shows that the bnei haneviim lost their prophecy, while Elisha received a double portion. He brings the Satmar Rav's own sefer: when the tzaddik's Torah is learned and one attaches to him it is not death of tzaddikim; it is only when his wisdom is lost.

title.en: The sweetness of his chiddushei Torah

summary.en: The Rav urges learning the Satmar Rav's sefarim, full of guidance in avodas Hashem and of chiddushim whose sweetness makes one smile, 'sweeter than honey'. He describes his total mastery of Torah and explains with 'pikudei Hashem yesharim mesamchei lev' that a chiddush that gladdens the heart is a sign of Torah lishmah.

title.en: Kedushas habris and the power of his words

summary.en: The Rav describes the Satmar Rav as a tzaddik of earlier generations: great tzaddikim attested to his purity, he did not sleep in a bed except Friday night, and once at three in the morning he was seen learning. In the Shovavim weeks his words on kedushas habris brought thousands to tears, because one can only give others what one has oneself.

title.en: Bereishis, the Aseres HaDibros, the Megillah and Ahavah Rabbah

summary.en: The Rav recounts hearing the Satmar Rav lain 'Bereishis' so that even the walls felt Hashem creating the world, and the crowds, including the elderly Rabbi Yonasan Steif, pushing to hear the Aseres HaDibros. He describes his Megillah reading, brings the story of Rabbi Shalom of Belz reading the Megillah before the Chozeh of Lublin, and his long Ahavah Rabbah, recalling the Ba'al Shem Tov that Moshiach tarries because people do not lengthen it.

title.en: A refined body: cherries, Shabbos fish, a changed face

summary.en: The Rav describes how the Satmar Rav's body was refined: seen through the blinds eating cherries on a Motzaei Shabbos with kavanos, eating not the fish but the Shabbos at his tish, and arranging the fish in a way Rabbi Yonasan Steif saw as holy names. His face changed so much on Shabbos, Pesach and hakafos that one could have taken him for another person.

title.en: Simchas Yom Tov and the freshness of Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav explains 'u'smachtem lifnei Hashem shivas yamim' through the Satmar Rav's long na'anuim with the lulav, which filled the beis medrash with joy and chen, which Rashi ties to Yosef's guarding of the bris. On Chanukah every night was for him like the first, which the Rav connects to his answering the Beis Yosef's question each night.

title.en: Torah from a holy mouth, and tzedakah

summary.en: With 'Torah yevakshu mipihu' the Rav explains that Torah from a holy person is a different Torah; one went to hear the Satmar Rav test his students to sense Torah lishmah, and he adds that children should be given to a melamed who is a yerei shamayim. He then describes how the Satmar Rav taught Williamsburg to give tzedakah beyond its means, even a week's wages at an appeal.

title.en: His last instruction: kohanim, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai

summary.en: At the levayah the Rav heard that one of the Satmar Rav's last instructions was that kohanim not enter the beis medrash. He explains the dispute whether tzaddikim impart tumah, the Yismach Moshe's view, and reads Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai's last words 'clear the vessels because of tumah and prepare a chair for Chizkiyahu' as a ruling that tzaddikim do impart tumah, with Chizkiyahu, master of tumah and taharah, coming to greet him.

title.en: Purity in the camp and the Rambam's Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav tells from a survivor's article how the Satmar Rav kept clean in the concentration camp and kept his beard. He explains that great tzaddikim sensed he could have led toward Moshiach, as with Chizkiyahu and Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai, but the 'biryonim' spoiled it; he reads the Rambam's description of Moshiach as the pure Moshiach the Satmar Rav wanted.

title.en: Belief in Moshiach owed to the Satmar Rav

summary.en: The Rav says that today's belief in the coming of Moshiach is owed to the Satmar Rav, who alone cried out when many called the state the geulah, and he tells of a speech at a Mizrachi convention asking prayers for his health. He compares him to Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai, who asked for Yavneh and was called a traitor yet was the true 'doresh l'Tzion'.

title.en: True lover of Zion, and the Kosel ruling

summary.en: The Rav calls the Satmar Rav the true lover of Zion who could tolerate no stain on the geulah. He explains his ruling against going to the Kosel, which was not generally accepted, with the Gemara of Rav Ketina mocking a necromancer so that people would not be drawn after him: the ruling protected even those who go.

title.en: Levi, the last of the Shevatim

summary.en: The Rav calls the Satmar Rav a tzaddik of earlier generations and laments the orphaned generation left like a small boat in the sea. He paints the scene of Levi, the last of the Shevatim, telling the Jews in Egypt about Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, and their despair at his passing; the Midrash on 'Yosef and all his brothers died' answers that the One Above did not die, and he adds that Shimshon's might outlived him.

title.en: Following the footsteps of the flock

summary.en: The Rav brings the Pesikta that the tzaddikim of the churban are greater than those of the binyan, relative to what is expected of their generation. With 'tz'i lach b'ikvei hatzon' he says that whoever holds to the tzaddikim's mesorah and learns their Torah keeps them alive; he ends with hashgachah, emunah until Moshiach, and blessings for the new year.

catalogTitle: שמיטה: שנה של התפשטות ירושלים על כל א"י וכל יהודי נעשה ללוי (שייכות ליו"ט סוכות)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Yerushalayim is always in a state of shemitah, that in the seventh year its holiness spreads over all of Eretz Yisrael and every Jew becomes like a Levi, and that the sukkah brings a Jew into Yerushalayim wherever he is.

abstract.en: The Rav opens on Sukkos, whose center is Shemini Atzeres, when the Torah reading speaks of shemitah. Shemitah teaches that a Jew is a stranger: his field and his money are not his own. Using olam, shanah and nefesh, he explains that Yerushalayim is the Shabbos of place as shemitah is the Shabbos of time: Yerushalayim was never divided among the tribes, its houses are not rented, nothing is planted there, and it belongs to Hashem. In the seventh year Yerushalayim spreads over all of Eretz Yisrael and every Jew becomes like the tribe of Levi. Shemitah is therefore a tosefes, an addition to Yerushalayim, which is why Rabbi Akiva learns tosefes from it. Finally the sukkah is Yerushalayim and the Holy of Holies; entering it is like fleeing to Eretz Yisrael, which reopens a verdict. He closes with the 122 days from Elul to Zos Chanukah, a call not to waste them, and words on the geulah of a lowly generation.

en: Shemitah teaches that a Jew is a stranger in this world: his field and even his money are not his own, and he must trust Hashem.
Yerushalayim is the Shabbos of place just as shemitah is the Shabbos of time, so in Yerushalayim it is always shemitah.
In the seventh year Yerushalayim spreads over all of Eretz Yisrael, and every Jew becomes like the tribe of Levi, without a field of his own.
Shemitah is not something new but a continuation and tosefes of Yerushalayim, and so it is the root of every tosefes, including tosefes Shabbos.
The sukkah is Yerushalayim and the Holy of Holies, so a Jew who enters it is like one who flees to Eretz Yisrael, where his verdict is reopened.
The 122 pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu match the 122 days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah, and these days must not be wasted.

candidateTopics: Yerushalayim as the Shabbos of place
spreading of Yerushalayim over Eretz Yisrael
the days of judgment until Zos Chanukah

title.en: Shemini Atzeres and the lesson of shemitah

summary.en: The Rav opens on Sukkos and says that all the Yamim Tovim revolve around Shemini Atzeres, when the Torah reading speaks of shemitah. He explains that shemitah teaches a Jew that he is a stranger whose field and money are not his own, and that he must trust Hashem.

title.en: Yerushalayim, the Shabbos of place

summary.en: Using olam, shanah and nefesh from Sefer Yetzirah, the Rav shows that the Holy of Holies, Yom Kippur and the Kohen Gadol meet on one day, and that Yerushalayim is the Shabbos of place as shemitah is the Shabbos of time. In Yerushalayim it is always shemitah, and in the seventh year it spreads over all of Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: Yerushalayim belongs to no one

summary.en: The Rav compares shemitah and Shabbos, which are 'for Hashem', with Yerushalayim, which has nothing of its own: nothing is planted there, it was not divided among the tribes, and its houses are not rented. Like a kallah who receives everything, the land is Hashem's; Yerushalayim is a place of Torah, and in the seventh year its state flows over all of Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: Yaakov, the tribes and Levi

summary.en: The Rav traces Klal Yisrael from the individual Avos to Yaakov, the trunk of the tree, from whom the twelve tribes branch out. Yaakov is Shabbos and the tribes are the weekday Roshei Chodesh; Eretz Yisrael was divided among the tribes, but Yerushalayim belongs to the trunk, and Levi, who has no portion, is shemitah. In shemitah every Jew becomes like a Levi, a taste of the World to Come.

title.en: Eating Shabbos, eating shemitah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the eating of Shabbos carries great holiness and tells of chassidim whose Shabbos fish and challah held Shabbos itself. He then shows that in shemitah one eats 'yashan', the old, like the 'atika' of Shabbos, and that eating shemitah fruits brings yiras Shamayim and puts a Jew into Yerushalayim even outside it.

title.en: Shemitah as the root of tosefes

summary.en: The Rav says shemitah brings nothing new; it is Yerushalayim flowing over, a tosefes like tosefes Shabbos. He brings Rabbi Akiva's teaching in Rosh Hashanah that tosefes is learned from shemitah, asks why the passuk begins with Shabbos and ends with shemitah, and answers that shemitah is itself the tosefes of Yerushalayim and so the root of every tosefes.

title.en: Rabbi Akiva, the man of additions

summary.en: The Rav brings from his rebbe, Reb Gedalya Schorr, that every mitzvah has a point that spreads to all mitzvos, as parah adumah is the root of every chok; shemitah is the root of tosefes. Rabbi Akiva, who descended from converts, who are an addition to Klal Yisrael, expounded the crowns on the letters and taught tosefes from shemitah.

title.en: Shemitah for Jews outside the land

summary.en: Shemitah, like Shabbos, is a kallah and carries a scent of the geulah, when Eretz Yisrael will spread over the whole world. The Rav explains that its holiness cannot rest on the land of chutz la'aretz, which belongs to the nations, but it does rest on the Jew there and on his money, as Reb Tzadok shows from the donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair.

title.en: The sukkah as Eretz Yisrael and Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that one sentenced who flees to Eretz Yisrael has his verdict reopened, and the seforim that the sukkah holds the air of Eretz Yisrael. He brings the Radomsker's question on 'in the place Hashem will choose', and the Sar Shalom of Belz: Sukkos is Yaakov, to whom Yerushalayim came in chutz la'aretz, so a Jew in a sukkah anywhere is in Yerushalayim.

title.en: Fleeing into the sukkah reopens the verdict

summary.en: The Rav brings that the sukkah joins the names Havayah and Adnus, like the keruvim spreading their wings over the kapores, so sitting in the sukkah is sitting in the Holy of Holies. A Jew who flees into the sukkah after Yom Kippur is like one who flees to Eretz Yisrael, where Hashem Himself judges, and there is only mercy.

title.en: This year and the sukkah's protection

summary.en: The Rav says that this year, 5768, Sukkos and shemitah meet, a double holiness of Yerushalayim, and that it is a year spoken of as fit for geulah. He explains that the segulah of the sukkah is protection, tells how the Belzer Rav stood at the Shabbos candles for hours during a war saying 'ufros aleinu sukkas shelomecha', and urges keeping the sukkah with all its hiddurim.

title.en: The 122 days and Parshas Ki Savo

summary.en: The Rav brings that the time of judgment extends to Hoshana Rabbah and, from the Arizal, to Zos Chanukah, and tells how the Maggid of Mezritch tested a new ba'al korei on how the parshiyos relate to the week. The pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu hint at these days, 122 in all, and Ki Savo is a mussar on the 122 days of the past year that were wasted.

title.en: The world needs a reckoning

summary.en: The Rav says the whole world, America as well as Eretz Yisrael, needs a reckoning. He tells how, when he was in Eretz Yisrael some years earlier, he answered someone afraid of the intifada that he was afraid to go to America, and soon after his return came the Twin Towers, as a Gemara about a plague in Eretz Yisrael implies. Now Hashem has given the sukkah and new 122 days, and one must not wait.

title.en: Geulah through the lowly generation

summary.en: The Rav says the geulah will not come through the greatness of the great generations but through the lowliness of the last one, like the aravah, the lowest of the minim. As Simchas Torah joins the end of the Torah to Bereishis, the lowly generation will be joined to Moshiach, and he closes with blessings for a good year.

catalogTitle: The Seven Middos of Sefirah; The קדושה of כלל ישראל vs. the טומאה of ישמעאל

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the seven middos that are refined during the seven weeks of Sefirah, and shows that Yishmael is the klipah of Yesod, which is why the present galus brings such hard tests of kedushah and why guarding that kedushah decides the struggle over Eretz Yisroel.

abstract.en: The Rav sets out to explain, in simple pshat, what the seven weeks of Sefirah are about. Hashem's attributes come down into this world in reduced form, like steam becoming water and ice, and appear as seven middos in every person, each usable for good or bad. He goes through chesed, gevurah, tiferes, netzach, hod, yesod and malchus, with their Avos, limbs and examples, and explains that each week one middah is to be purified. He then sets the seven Ushpizim against seven forces of tumah and turns to Yishmael: the Rambam's Iggeres Teiman calls them haters of peace, and the Zohar explains that their empty milah gave them Eretz Yisroel only while it was empty. Yishmael is the klipah of yesod, the one who sold Yosef to Mitzrayim, the ervas ha'aretz. The present summer's tests of tznius are part of a heavenly din Torah over Eretz Yisroel, decided in the yeshivos by Torah, tefillah and guarding the eyes.

en: The seven middos in a person are reduced forms of Hashem's attributes, the same substance in a more physical form, like steam, water and ice.
Each middah can be used for avodas Hashem or for the wrong things, and each of the seven weeks of Sefirah is given to purify one middah in preparation for Matan Torah.
Just as seven Ushpizim embody the seven middos in kedushah, seven nations embody them in tumah, and Yishmael is the klipah of yesod.
Yishmael held Eretz Yisroel through the galus only because his empty milah earned him the land while it stood empty; now that Jews are returning, that claim is being contested.
The present era is the time of the klipah of yesod, which is why the tests of tznius grow harder every summer.
The heavenly din Torah over Eretz Yisroel is decided in the yeshivos and batei medrash, through Torah, tefillah and guarding the eyes and thoughts.

title.en: Seven middos, from heaven to man

summary.en: The Rav opens by saying many count Sefirah without knowing what the words mean, and promises a simple pshat. He explains that Hashem's attributes come down reduced, with the mashal of steam, water and ice, and that of the ten maamaros seven came down into this world and into a person's character.

title.en: No reshus: every act is mitzvah or aveirah

summary.en: The Rav explains that a person can use his seven middos for avodas Hashem or for aveiros, since there is no neutral reshus. Eating for health to serve Hashem is a mitzvah, while indulging even in kosher food is what the Ramban on this week's sedrah condemns; the seven weeks are given to sanctify one middah each week.

title.en: Chesed, gevurah and tiferes

summary.en: The Rav explains chesed as ahavah, linked to Avraham and Pesach's Shir HaShirim; gevurah as yirah and pachad Yitzchak, with the example of a dayan wrongly afraid of a powerful litigant; and tiferes as harmony and pride, shown by a sunset and music, which belongs only with Hashem.

title.en: Netzach, hod, yesod and malchus

summary.en: The Rav matches the middos to the limbs and explains netzach as fighting to win and hod as yielding, the two legs on which a person stands; yesod as the drive for continuity, tied to bris milah; and malchus as bitul to Hashem, the middah of Shabbos and David HaMelech. He then says that the week of netzach starting that night means rising against the yetzer hara.

title.en: Gevurah within chesed, and Kedoshim tihyu

summary.en: The Rav explains that each middah has subdivisions, illustrating gevurah shebechesed with a mother who holds her baby tightly on the stairs out of love. He explains the request after counting that the flaw in that day's middah be repaired, and brings Rashi and the Ramban on Kedoshim tihyu.

title.en: Yishmael, the hater of peace

summary.en: The Rav sets the seven Ushpizim against the seven nations of Canaan as the middos in tumah, then turns to the Rambam's Iggeres Teiman, which calls the galus of Yishmael harder than that of Edom. He explains from the passuk about the tents of Kedar that Yishmael hates peace, and applies it to the current conflict.

title.en: Yishmael's empty milah and Eretz Yisroel

summary.en: The Rav asks why only Yishmael has held Eretz Yisroel since the Churban, and brings the Zohar: Yishmael's angel claimed the land for keeping milah, and was told his milah is empty, so he would hold the land while it is empty. He explains that Yishmael's middah is yesod in tumah, bringing the Gemara that nine of ten measures of znus went to Yishmael.

title.en: Azazel and the Kohen Gadol's miracle

summary.en: From the Yom Kippur reading the Rav explains that the sins are placed on Esav because a Jew's inner will is to do Hashem's will and the yetzer hara, Esav's angel, causes the sin, as shown by the Rambam on compelling a person until he says he wants. He then brings the Tosfos Yom Tov's answer why it was a miracle that the Kohen Gadol never became tamei on Yom Kippur: the Satan concentrated all his power on him.

title.en: Yishmael, Yosef and Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Rav explains what a klipah is with the mashal of a peel, and that Yishmael, the klipah of yesod, pursues Yosef, the tzaddik of yesod: it was Yishmaelim who sold Yosef to Mitzrayim. Using the three dimensions of place, time and soul, he calls Mitzrayim the place of the klipah of yesod, the ervas ha'aretz, as against Tziyon.

title.en: The time of the klipah of yesod

summary.en: The Rav asks why each summer the tests of tznius grow harder, recalling how different the street was when he was a boy, and answers that the end of galus is galus Yishmael, the time of the klipah of yesod. He explains that the world's focus on Eretz Yisroel reflects a din Torah in Shamayim, fought not by armies but in the yeshivos through Torah, tefillah and guarding the eyes.

title.en: The geulah is in the bochur's hands

summary.en: The Rav concludes that a Jew who turns his eyes away fights the war against Yishmael, and that the geulah depends not on Washington but on Torah, tefillah, tzedakah and guarding yesod. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar that all of Sefirah is about rectifying yesod, recalls how Yosef's kedushah saved the Jews in Mitzrayim, and ends with a wish that the bochurim pass the summer's test and bring Moshiach.

catalogTitle: מאכלות אסורות: דרוש בענין: גודל הפגם של מאכלות האסורות ותיקון למי שנפגם בזה (שייכות לסוכות ושמ"ע ופרשת ראה)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why forbidden food does such deep damage, dulling the heart and cutting a Jew's felt bond with Hashem, and shows from the order of parshas Re'eh that the repair is holy eating and wholehearted teshuvah, which is why the end of Re'eh is read on Shemini Atzeres.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Sukkos as a return to Gan Eden after Yom Kippur's atonement for Adam's sin, and Shemini Atzeres as the peak of all the Yamim Tovim, which needs a teshuvah greater than Yom Kippur. He then lays out parshas Re'eh: it opens with eating kodshim in Yerushalayim, turns to the meisis and the forbidden animals, and returns to aser te'aser. Eating is the gravest act because food becomes part of the person; forbidden food dulls the heart and breaks the felt bond with Hashem. He illustrates that bond with the halacha of a bas Levi, the Lechovitcher's cry and Baal Peor, and brings the Bnei Yissaschar that even one damaged through his parents can purify himself. A long discussion of Rosh Chodesh, melacha as Adam's curse and women's sensitivity follows. He ends that holy eating, the Shabbos table and wholehearted teshuvah on Shemini Atzeres repair the damage.

en: Eating is graver than other acts because the food becomes part of the person, and forbidden food dulls the heart so that one no longer feels kedushah or has desire to learn and daven.
Parshas Re'eh opens with holy eating in Yerushalayim, moves to the meisis and the forbidden animals, and returns to aser te'aser; the middle is the damage and the end is the repair.
A Jew who truly feels his bond with Hashem cannot be talked away by a meisis; one who falls has lost that feeling, and the Torah traces it to forbidden food.
Even someone damaged through no fault of his own, through what his parents fed him, has no excuse: by strengthening himself with all his strength in avodas Hashem he can purify himself completely.
The repair of the damage is holy eating in a holy place: the Shabbos table, eating together with Jews, the sukkah, netilas yadayim and bentching with kavanah.
Shemini Atzeres, a day of love after the awe of the Yamim Noraim, is a time of teshuvah with the whole heart, and that is why the closing parsha of Re'eh is read on it.
